title: Wallets, Keys & Self-Custody
description: The second Basic course. You already know that a private key is power of attorney over coins. This course is the operating manual: what a wallet actually is, custodial versus self-custody, how a seed phrase works, how to receive and send on BNB Smart Chain without mixing networks, how approvals drain wallets, and how to store a backup like an adult. Education only — practice with amounts you can lose. Crystal Stones Academy will never ask for a seed phrase.

modules.description: A wallet is a key manager, not a bank drawer. Separate the app, the PIN, the keys, and the chain.

lessons.title: A wallet does not hold coins
lessons.content:
# A wallet does not hold coins

The word **wallet** is a bad metaphor, and it is the first one this course has to kill. A leather wallet holds cash. A crypto wallet does **not** hold coins. If you keep that picture, every later lesson will fight you.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to point at a phone screen and say, in your own words, where the coins actually live, what the app is doing, and what you lose if the phone dies. You already met **keys** in Crypto Foundations: a private key is power of attorney over coins. This course is the operating manual for that fact.

## Coins live on the chain, not in the icon

A **blockchain** is a public book of balances and transfers. **BNB Smart Chain** is one such book. Its chain id is **56**. Its common explorer is **BscScan**. The native coin that pays fees on that book is **BNB**.

When a wallet app shows “0.12 BNB,” it is not showing you notes stuffed inside the app. It is showing you what the book currently lists for an **address** that the app can sign for. Uninstall the app and the book does not empty. Smash the phone and the book does not empty. The book changes only when a valid signed instruction is accepted.

That is the whole mental model, and beginners fight it for months. They say “my Trust Wallet has the coins.” Trust Wallet is an **example of a wallet app**, not a vault in Cupertino. MetaMask is another example of a wallet app, usually living as a browser extension. Neither company is a bank drawer. Neither is this academy’s product.

If the only copy of the keys lived inside that dead phone, and you have no backup, you did not “lose the coins from the app.” You lost the **power of attorney**. The coins are still on the book, sitting at an address nobody you know can move. That is a worse outcome than a stolen leather wallet, because there is no branch manager who can reprint the notes.

## Three jobs a wallet actually does

A wallet, used honestly, is a **key manager**. It does three jobs:

1. It stores or uses your **keys** (or asks a hardware device to use them).
2. It builds **transactions** — signed instructions the network can check.
3. It shows you a human picture of what the book says.

Job 3 is a **report**. Reports can lag. Reports can be drawn by a fake app. Reports can show a token that is a clone. The book is still the book. Later in this module you will treat explorers as the adult copy of the report. Today you only need this: the screen is not the money.

**Transaction** means a message that says, roughly: “the holder of this key authorises this movement under these rules.” It is not a chat receipt. It is not a WhatsApp screenshot. It is not “I meant to pay you.” After the network accepts it and later pages bury it, there is no academy help desk that can reverse it.

TABLE
Everyday sentence | What is actually true | What you risk if you believe the sentence
“The coins are in my wallet app” | The coins are rows on the chain; the app is a window and a pen | You think uninstalling the app deletes the money, or that reinstalling magically restores keys you never backed up
“I lost my wallet when the phone drowned” | You lost the device, maybe the only copy of the keys | You wait for Apple or Google to “recover crypto”
“The app balance is the official truth” | The chain is the official truth; the app asked a helper and drew a number | You argue from a screenshot instead of an explorer row
“Crystal Stones lives inside Crystal Stones Academy” | Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 token on BNB Smart Chain | You send tokens to a random academy “portal”
ENDTABLE

## What happens when the phone dies

**Worked scenario.** Amaka’s phone falls in a basin of water. The Trust Wallet icon is gone. She still has twelve words on a paper in a drawer.

1. She buys a new phone from a shop she chose, not from a stranger who “already installed the wallet for her.”
2. She installs the **official** app from the official store — the same publisher she used before, not a clone with a similar name.
3. She chooses Restore / Import, and types the twelve words **into that app once**, privately, not into a website, not into a Telegram bot.
4. The app derives the same keys, asks BNB Smart Chain what those addresses hold, and draws the same balances.
5. The coins did not “come back from the cloud.” The app asked the book again. The book still listed those addresses.

If the words existed only on the dead phone, the vault combination is gone. No academy mentor, no “recovery agent,” no remote-desktop helper can honestly fetch them. Anyone who says they can is selling a second theft.

DIAGRAM
BNB Smart Chain (the book)
        ^
        |  reads balances, broadcasts signed transactions
        |
Wallet app (the window and the pen)
        ^
        |  unlocked by PIN / fingerprint on THIS device
        |
Keys / seed phrase (the vault combination)

Phone dies: window is gone.
Paper backup exists: combination still works in a new window.
No backup: combination is gone. The book still lists the coins. Nobody you know can move them.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why the metaphor still exists, and how this academy will use the word

Early Bitcoin used “wallet” because people needed a word that felt like money. The industry kept it. You will keep hearing it in shops, in WhatsApp groups, and on YouTube. Inside this academy, when we say **wallet** we mean **key manager**, unless we explicitly say **custodial account** (an exchange login, which is an IOU in a company’s ledger).

Crystal Stones’ token, as a **BEP-20** asset on BNB Smart Chain, is a row in **that** book. A wallet that can speak BNB Smart Chain can show it **if** you are looking at the right contract and the right network. A Bitcoin-only wallet will not magically display a BEP-20 token. Wrong book. The public Crystal Stones contract, as the project publishes it, is:

`0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`

Treat that as a **reference to verify**, not a request to buy, and not something to type into a random “add token” website a stranger sent you. This academy will not tell you to buy Crystal Stones to finish this course. You can complete every lab with a practice amount of BNB you can afford to lose, or even with an empty wallet and a paper drill.

NOTE
Academy staff will never ask you to “import your wallet into our portal.” Importing a seed into a website is how wallets empty. There is no academy portal that needs those words, your private key, your 2FA codes, or remote desktop control of your phone. If a message uses our name and asks for any of those, it is theft wearing a logo.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You are not here to worship an app brand. You are here so that “wallet,” “keys,” “chain,” and “balance” stop being one mashed object. The rest of Basic — exchanges, BNB Smart Chain, safety — assumes you can point at the right object. If you still think coins live in the icon, stop and reread. The metaphor is the trap.

## Say this out loud

- Coins live on the chain. The wallet is a window and a pen, not a drawer of notes.
- Uninstalling an app is not the same as losing keys — unless the keys had no backup.
- A drowned phone with a paper seed is an inconvenience. A drowned phone with no backup is a closed vault.
- A BEP-20 token is invisible to a wallet pointed at the wrong network.
- Crystal Stones Academy will never ask for a seed phrase, a private key, a 2FA code, or remote screen control.

Next: four objects people smash into the single word “wallet” — the app, the device lock, the keys, and the chain.

lessons.title: Four objects people smash into one word
lessons.content:
# Four objects people smash into one word

People say “wallet” and mean four different objects. Then they treat a fingerprint as a seed, treat an app PIN as chain insurance, and treat a network dropdown as decoration. This lesson separates the four objects until you can name which one you are touching.

By the end you should be able to look at a phone and say: that icon is the app, that Face ID is the device lock, those twelve words are the keys, and that BNB number is a row on a chain. Mixing them is how ordinary adults lose money without a “hacker genius” in the story.

## Object 1 — the wallet app

The **wallet app** is a program. Trust Wallet on a phone is an example of a wallet app. MetaMask in a browser is an example of a wallet app. A hardware device’s companion app on a laptop is also an app. Programs have bugs, updates, phishing clones, and app-store fakes.

An app can be deleted and reinstalled. That is not a chain event. If you still hold the keys, a clean official install is a new window on the same book. If you install a clone with a similar icon from a random APK site, the clone’s job is to harvest the words you type. The clone will still draw a pretty balance. Pretty is not proof.

Apps also choose which **networks** they speak. A Bitcoin-only app will not show Crystal Stones. An app that can add **EVM** networks — Ethereum-style chains that use 0x addresses — can speak BNB Smart Chain if you set it to do so. The app is a translator. It is not the book.

## Object 2 — the device lock

The **device lock** is the PIN, pattern, fingerprint, or face that opens **this phone or this browser profile**. It is local security. It stops a thief who picks up an unlocked handset for thirty seconds. It does **not** live on BNB Smart Chain.

Resetting a PIN does not reset the book. Factory-resetting a phone does not notify validators. Apple or Google unlocking a new handset for you does not reprint a seed you never wrote down. The device lock and the vault combination are different secrets with different jobs.

Beginners mash them because both feel like “my password.” Say it the long way until it sticks: the PIN is the lock on this furniture. The seed is the combination of the vault the furniture was looking at.

## Object 3 — the keys

The **keys** are the secret that can **sign**. In practice you meet them as a **seed phrase** (12 or 24 words) and as **private keys** derived from that seed. Module 2 of this course is entirely about this object. Today you only need the job description: whoever can use the keys can spend the coins. There is no “dear blockchain, that was not me.”

A **signature** is mathematics that proves the holder of the secret authorised this message, without putting the secret in the message. The network checks the signature. It does not check your national ID. It does not check whether you were tired, phished, or helping an auntie.

## Object 4 — the chain

The **chain** is the book. BNB Smart Chain, Bitcoin, Ethereum, and the rest are separate books. Your wallet app can speak to several books. That does not make the books the same. Balances do not spill across them because the address **looks** similar.

On BNB Smart Chain, **BNB** is the native coin that pays **gas** (the network fee). **BEP-20** tokens — Crystal Stones, USDT on BSC, and others — are entries in token contracts on that same book. Moving a token still spends BNB. The chain does not care that your local currency account is empty. It cares that the sending address can pay the fee.

TABLE
Object | Everyday picture | What it can do | If you lose it
Wallet app | The banking-app icon | Draw balances, propose transactions | Reinstall from the official store; keys can restore the view
Device lock | The lock on this phone | Stop a grab-and-run on this device | Annoying. Not a chain reset. Not a seed
Seed / private key | The vault combination | Sign. Spend. Empty the address | Coins can be spent by whoever has it. No help desk
Chain record | The official book | Decide what is paid | Still there even if your phone dies
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Jordan’s cousin picks up his unlocked phone and opens the wallet app. There is no PIN on the app itself — only the phone’s lock, which was already off.

1. The cousin can see addresses and balances. That is object 4, reported by object 1.
2. If the app still has the keys unlocked (object 3 sitting ready), the cousin can send.
3. Changing the phone PIN afterwards does not reverse the send. Object 2 is furniture. The book already moved.
4. If Jordan had used a hardware device, the cousin would still need that device and its own PIN. Different object, different grab.
5. If Jordan now factory-resets the phone “to be safe” without a seed backup, he has punished himself, not the cousin. The cousin already signed. The reset only destroys the remaining copy of the keys.

DIAGRAM
You say “wallet”
        |
        +--> App (program, clone risk, network list)
        +--> Device lock (PIN / face — this furniture only)
        +--> Keys / seed (the only thing that can sign)
        +--> Chain (BNB Smart Chain, chain id 56, BscScan)

Touch the wrong object, tell the wrong story, take the wrong recovery step.
ENDDIAGRAM

## How the four objects show up on one screen

Open a typical phone wallet and you will see all four at once, mashed:

- An icon and a brand name (app).
- A prompt for fingerprint when you open it (device lock, or the app’s own PIN — still local).
- A “Backup” nag about twelve words (keys).
- A number labelled BNB or a token name (chain report).

The **network selector** is part of the app, but it chooses which chain you are reading. If it says Ethereum, you are looking at Ethereum’s book. If it says BNB Smart Chain, you are looking at BSC. The same seed can produce an address that **looks** the same on both, because both are EVM-style. The **balances are not shared**. USDT on Ethereum is not USDT on BSC. Crystal Stones on BSC is not “whatever token a clone deployed on another chain.”

NOTE
When this academy says “protect your wallet,” we will try to say which object. Protect the app by installing it from the official store. Protect the device with a lock. Protect the keys with a paper or steel backup you never photograph. Protect your reading of the chain by checking BscScan, not a screenshot. A sentence that does not name the object is a slogan.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have names for the four objects. The rest of this module uses them without apology. Custodial versus self-custody is about **who holds object 3**. Hot versus cold is about **where object 3 sits**. The screen versus the book is about **object 1 lying about object 4**. If you cannot name the object, stop moving value.

## Say this out loud

- “Wallet” is four objects: app, device lock, keys, and chain.
- A PIN or fingerprint locks this device. It does not reset the book and it is not the seed.
- Keys sign. Whoever can sign can spend. The chain does not parent you.
- The network dropdown chooses which book you are reading. Same 0x shape is not a shared piggy bank.
- Reinstalling an official app restores a view only if you still have the keys.

Next: three honest ways to “have” crypto — custodial, software self-custody, and hardware — and why mixing the stories is how funds disappear.

lessons.title: Custodial, self-custody, and hardware
lessons.content:
# Custodial, self-custody, and hardware

There are three honest ways to “have” crypto. None is morally superior. **Mixing them up** is how people lose everything and then write “the blockchain stole my money.”

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name which of the three you are using, every time you look at a balance. If you cannot name it, you do not know who can freeze you, who can spend, and who you call when something breaks.

## 1. Custodial — you have an account

**Custodial** means a company holds the keys. An **exchange** or a fintech app holds them. You log in with email, password, maybe SMS or an authenticator app. What you see is a **balance in their ledger**.

Binance is **an example of a centralised exchange**, not “the only real one.” A local P2P desk that credits you inside their own app is also custodial. Your local currency fintech wallet is custodial too: a company book, not BNB Smart Chain.

This is useful:

- changing local currency into USDT or BNB
- when you do not yet want to hold a seed
- when a court or a company *should* be able to freeze an account (that is a feature of this design, not a bug you discovered late)

This is the cost:

- they can freeze withdrawals
- a phishing site can steal the login
- if the company fails, you are in a queue of creditors, not holding keys

**“I have USDT on Binance”** means: Binance’s book says they owe you. Until you **withdraw** to an address you control, you hold an **IOU**. An IOU can be honest and still not be self-custody. Both facts can be true. This academy will not order you off every exchange on day one. It will order you to stop calling an IOU a key.

## 2. Self-custody (software) — you hold the keys on a phone or browser

**Self-custody** means you can sign. The seed lives (encrypted) on the device. Trust Wallet, MetaMask, and similar apps are **examples of wallet apps** that can do this. They are not endorsements. They are not academy products.

This is useful:

- you can leave an exchange
- you can talk to **dApps** — decentralized apps, meaning websites that ask the wallet to sign
- Crystal Stones, as a BEP-20 token, can show up when the network is BNB Smart Chain and you have added the right contract

This is the cost:

- malware
- fake apps in the store
- a photo of the seed in Google Photos
- signing a malicious contract because a website asked nicely

**Hot wallet** means: the keys sit on a machine that also goes online. Convenient. Attackable. A phone that has Telegram, WhatsApp, Chrome, and a wallet is a hot environment even if you are a careful person. Care is not architecture.

## 3. Hardware — the keys sit in a dedicated device

Ledger and Trezor are **examples of hardware wallets**, not ads, not a homework purchase for this week. The seed is generated and stored inside a small computer that does not browse the web. The computer signs; the laptop only proposes.

This is useful:

- amounts you would actually miss
- a backup that is not “a screenshot”

This is the cost:

- you can still be phished (you sign the wrong thing on the device screen)
- you can lose the device **and** the paper backup
- cheap clones exist; buy from the maker, not a random marketplace listing with a seed already in the box

**Cold** means: the keys are not on an internet-connected general-purpose computer. Hardware is the common beginner form of cold. A paper backup of a seed is also cold — and also easy to photograph, flood, or fight over in a family. Module 5 returns to hardware without worship. Today you only need to place it on the map.

TABLE
Style | What you actually have | Who can freeze it | Typical fail
Custodial exchange | A login and an IOU | The company, a court, a fraud team | Freeze, hack of the company, phishing the email
Software self-custody | Keys on a phone or browser | Nobody at a help desk — only you, or whoever stole the seed | Fake app, clipboard malware, seed photo
Hardware self-custody | Keys in a dedicated box | Still nobody at a help desk | Tampered device, signing a malicious tx, lost backup
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Sam, a freelancer in Lagos, buys a little USDT on an exchange, leaves it there, and tells friends “I am in self-custody now.” She is not.

1. She has an account. The exchange can still freeze withdrawals if a compliance flag fires.
2. Self-custody starts at **withdraw to an address whose seed she holds**.
3. She later withdraws 10 USDT as a test on **BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20)** to a wallet she created herself.
4. She checks BscScan for the incoming transfer to **her** address, not a screenshot from the exchange chat support.
5. Only then does she have a small self-custodied balance. The rest still sitting on the exchange is still an IOU. Leaving it there is a legitimate choice. It is not self-custody.

DIAGRAM
Local currency (local currency, etc.)
        |
        v
Custodial on-ramp (exchange / P2P desk)
        |
        |  withdraw — this is the moment self-custody can begin
        v
Software wallet (hot)  ----optional---->  Hardware wallet (colder)
        |
        v
You can hold BNB + BEP-20 tokens, including Crystal Stones as a view
        |
        v
You can also send back to an exchange (re-entering custody on purpose)
ENDDIAGRAM

## Mixing the three stories is the actual disaster

The disaster is rarely “I chose custody.” The disaster is thinking an exchange password is a seed, thinking a hardware box makes a phishing site safe, depositing to an exchange using the wrong network then arguing with “the blockchain,” asking exchange support to restore a self-custody seed, or asking a wallet app’s Twitter to reverse an exchange freeze. Name the bucket before you name the blame.

This academy’s paid-track checkout, when you meet it later, is **USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout**. That is a payment rail, not Crystal Stones token, and not an instruction to hold anything. You will still need to know whether you are paying from an exchange withdrawal or from a wallet you control. Different objects, same sentence: asset, network, standard, from which kind of account.

Hardware does not cancel custody. If you buy a Ledger or a Trezor and then leave every coin on an exchange, you bought a signer you are not using. If you create a software wallet and then type the seed into an exchange “support form,” you converted self-custody into a gift. The object that matters is still: who can sign, right now.

NOTE
This course will not order you to buy a hardware wallet this week, and it will not order you to empty every exchange. It will order you to **name which of the three you are using**, every time you move value. If you cannot name it, stop. Moving value while confused is how post-mortems start.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have three honest buckets. Hot versus cold, in the next lesson, is a refinement of buckets 2 and 3. It is not a fourth religion. Practice saying the long sentence: “This is an IOU at a company” or “This is a key on my phone” or “This is a key in a dedicated device.” Short slogans hide the object.

## Say this out loud

- Custodial means an IOU from a company. Self-custody means you can sign. Hardware means the keys are not on the laptop.
- Withdrawal is the moment self-custody can begin. A balance on an exchange is not that moment.
- Hot means the keys can sign from an online daily driver. Cold means they cannot.
- Mixing the three stories is how people blame “the blockchain” for a company freeze or a seed photo.
- Ledger and Trezor are examples of hardware, not homework, not ads, and not magic.

Next: hot versus cold in more detail, and why “I wrote it in my Notes app” is still hot.

lessons.title: Hot, cold, and the Notes-app trap
lessons.content:
# Hot, cold, and the Notes-app trap

**Hot** and **cold** are about whether the secret sits on a machine that also talks to the internet. They are not a personality type. They are not a moral grade. A hardware wallet used to sign a phishing site is hot *in effect*: the attacker did not need to steal the chip. They needed your finger on the button.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to sort every copy of your seed into hot or cold, including the copies you pretend do not count — the photo “just for today,” the WhatsApp message to yourself, the email draft.

## Hot is convenient and noisy

Anything that can sign from a daily driver is hot: a browser extension; a phone wallet; a seed typed into a laptop that also has Telegram, Chrome, and random PDFs; a seed sitting in a cloud notes app that syncs to that laptop.

Hot wallets are how you **use** crypto: pay a fee, talk to a site, move a practice amount. They are not how you should store a year of savings on day two of this course. That is not a scare banner. It is a matching of tool to job. You do not leave a month of rent in the same pocket as your bus fare because both are “money.”

A **hot wallet** is still self-custody if you hold the keys. Self-custody and cold are not synonyms. You can hold keys on a noisy phone. That is self-custody and hot. An exchange is neither. Trust Wallet and MetaMask, as **examples of wallet apps**, are typically hot when they sit on a daily driver. That is not an insult. It is the job they are good at.

Hot also includes copies you did not mean to make. Android backups, iCloud Photos, WhatsApp media, Google Drive “scan document,” a printer job at a business centre. If a company computer can see the words, the words are hot. If a cousin can open the chat, the words are hot.

## Cold is quiet and easy to do badly

Cold examples: a hardware device bought from the maker and initialized by you; a seed written on paper or steel, never photographed, never typed into a computer except the device itself.

Fake cold — the Notes-app trap and its cousins: seed in iCloud Notes or Google Keep; seed in a WhatsApp “message to myself”; seed in an email draft; seed in a screenshot folder; seed in a password manager **shared with a teammate**; seed in a photo of the paper, because “my handwriting is ugly.”

Those copies live on company servers, or on a camera roll that backups to company servers. That is a hot backup wearing a paper costume. The paper in the drawer is not the copy that matters to an attacker. The synced copy is.

A paper backup can still fail as cold without a cloud: it sits in the same bag as the phone, so one theft takes both; it sits under a mattress in a house that burns; it is so cleverly hidden that you cannot find it either. Cold is a location and a process, not a vibe.

TABLE
Backup | Actually cold? | Why | Beginner verdict
Paper in a drawer, never photographed | Yes, if the house risk is acceptable | No server has a copy | Fine for practice amounts
Steel plate, two locations | Yes | Fire and flood resistant | For amounts you would miss, later
Notes app / Google Doc | No | Synced, searchable, account-takeover | Treat as leaked
Photo of the paper | No | Camera-roll backups | Treat as leaked
Password manager on your personal vault, no sharing | Debatable | Convenient, still an account to phish | Not this course’s default
Hardware device, seed never exported | Yes, for the keys in the chip | You still need a paper/steel backup of the seed | Optional later layer
WhatsApp “message to myself” | No | Chat backups, other devices, screenshot risk | Treat as leaked
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Yusuf “backs up” twelve words by emailing them to himself with the subject “crypto.” He also has them on paper.

1. Two years later his email is phished. The thief does not need the phone.
2. The thief restores the wallet in an hour on a fresh install of an official-looking app.
3. BscScan will show outgoing transfers signed by Yusuf’s key. The chain did nothing wrong.
4. The paper in the drawer is still there. It did not protect him, because a hotter copy existed.
5. The correct move, which Module 2 will drill, is **rotation**: new wallet, tiny test, move, retire the old words. Hoping “nobody looked” is not a control.

DIAGRAM
Real cold                              Fake cold

 Device / paper that never             Cloud note, screenshot,
 talks to random websites              chat backup, email draft
        |                                       |
        v                                       v
 Attacker must touch the               Attacker needs one
 physical object                       password reset or one
                                       malware scan of photos
ENDDIAGRAM

## Signing the wrong thing makes even hardware hot in effect

Cold storage is about **where the secret sits**. It is not a spell that blesses every click. If a website proposes a transaction that sends your tokens to a thief, and you confirm it on a hardware screen you did not read, the architecture did its job and you still paid the thief.

That is why this academy will keep repeating **read the sheet**. The wallet sheet — the popup that asks you to confirm — is the last place the true destination and the true permission show up. A pretty website is not that place. A Telegram admin is not that place.

If you already put a seed in the cloud, treat it as **leaked**. Not “maybe later.” Not “it was only a practice wallet.” Practice wallets become funded wallets because humans are lazy. Later in this course we cover rotation in full. Today’s rule is simpler: do not add a digital copy, and if one already exists, assume it is the copy that counts.

A related trap: writing the words in a phone note “until I get paper,” then forgetting to delete the note. Deleting a note that already synced is not time travel. The backup of the backup may still exist. Rotation is cleaner than archaeology.

People also confuse **encrypted** with **cold**. A notes app that claims encryption still lives behind an account you can phish, a device you already unlock to read WhatsApp, and a recovery email. Encryption of a hot copy is not the same architecture as a paper that never left the house.

NOTE
If you already put a seed in the cloud, treat it as leaked. Create a new wallet later in this course, prove the new backup, move a tiny test, then the rest, then retire the old words. Do not “hope nobody looked.” Hope is not a backup. Crystal Stones Academy will never offer to “store your seed for you” in a student portal, and will never ask you to screenshot words “so we can verify the backup.”
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now sort copies. The next lesson is about another lie: the screen versus the book. Hot and cold are about keys. Screens and books are about reports. Different objects. Do not mash them.

## Say this out loud

- Hot means keys can sign from an online daily driver. Cold means they are not sitting on that daily driver.
- A cloud copy of a seed is hot, even if a paper copy also exists. Attackers use the hotter copy.
- Signing the wrong thing makes even hardware hot in effect.
- A seed in Notes, WhatsApp, email, or photos is a leak wearing a backup costume.
- Self-custody and cold are not synonyms. You can hold keys and still be hot.

Next: the screen versus the book — why your app can lie, what a watch-only view is, and why a delayed RPC is not a theft.

lessons.title: The screen versus the book
lessons.content:
# The screen versus the book

A wallet screen is a **report**. The chain is the **book**. When they disagree, the book wins.

This lesson exists because scammers send screenshots, because honest apps lag, and because a **watch-only** address can look like a wallet that can spend. By the end you should be able to use an explorer as the adult copy of the report, and you should know what an RPC is without becoming an engineer.

## What the app is doing when it draws a number

Most phone wallets are **light clients**. They do not store the whole BNB Smart Chain. They ask a helper computer — an **RPC** — “what does this address hold?” Then they draw a number.

**RPC** means **Remote Procedure Call**: a way for your app to ask a node for chain data and to broadcast a signed transaction. You will see “RPC” in network settings. For BNB Smart Chain you want a helper that is actually talking to chain id **56**, not a lookalike chain with a similar name.

If the RPC is slow, your balance looks wrong. If the RPC is malicious, your balance can look right while a send goes somewhere else. If the app is a clone from a random APK site, it can draw whatever it wants while it steals the seed you just typed in. Three different failures. One screen. Name which failure you are in before you “fix” it by sending more.

**Delayed RPC** is the honest lag: you received BNB two minutes ago, the explorer shows it, the phone still shows 0.00. Pull to refresh. Switch off Wi-Fi and on again. Wait a block or two. Do not panic-send a second payment. Do not give a stranger remote access “to refresh the node.”

A light client is a design trade. You get a small app that runs on a phone. You pay for it by trusting a helper to tell you the truth and to broadcast your signed transaction. A **full node** would check the rules itself. You do not need to run one to finish Basic. You need to know that your pretty number came from a helper, not from a vault inside the icon.

TABLE
You see | What might be true | Adult move
“0.00” after a send to you | Tx still pending, RPC not refreshed, or wrong network in the app | Check BscScan on your address; wait; do not send twice
“Success” in a chat screenshot | Photoshop, or a send on a different chain | Paste the tx hash into the real explorer yourself
A token named Crystal Stones | Could be a clone contract with a similar name | Compare the contract to 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00
Green “connected” | Connected to a website. Not the same as “this website is honest” | Connecting is not paying and not approving
Watch-only / imported address | The app can see; it cannot sign unless keys are present | If it cannot send, you are looking, not holding
ENDTABLE

## The explorer is the adult move

A **block explorer** is a search engine for one chain’s book. For BNB Smart Chain, **BscScan** is the common one. Bookmark the real domain the way you bookmark a bank. Fake explorers exist. Never follow an explorer link from a random DM.

You will practise this until it is a reflex:

1. Copy the **transaction hash** (a long id the wallet shows after a send) or the **address**.
2. Paste it into the explorer **for that chain**.
3. Read the official row: asset, from, to, status, network, timestamp.

If the row is not there, it is not paid. An argument in Telegram is not a row. A JPEG is not a row. A customer who swears they paid is not a row.

Explorers can also lag, and fake explorers can lie. Two controls: you typed the domain from a bookmark, and you are looking at the address you actually control, not an address the sender chose for you. If two honest sources disagree, wait a minute. If a stranger’s screenshot disagrees with your bookmark, the stranger is not a source.

## Watch-only is a window without a pen

**Watch-only** (sometimes “address import” or “observation”) means the app knows an address and can draw its balances, but it does **not** have the keys. This is useful: a shopkeeper can watch a receiving address on a tablet that never held a seed. It is also how people fool themselves.

If you paste an address into a wallet and it shows Crystal Stones, you have not “imported the wallet.” You have imported a view. Pressing Send will fail or will ask for keys you do not have. Do not then type a seed into a second app “to make send work” on a device you do not trust.

**Worked scenario.** A buyer says they paid Amaka in Crystal Stones. They send a screenshot of a wallet with a green tick.

1. Amaka does not argue about JPEG quality.
2. She opens BscScan — the real site from her bookmark — and pastes **her** receiving address.
3. She filters the token to the Crystal Stones **contract** 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00.
4. If there is no incoming transfer, she was not paid. If there is a transfer of a **different** token named Crystal Stones, she was paid a clone. If the transfer is on another chain, she was paid on the wrong book.
5. Only if the explorer row matches asset, network, and her address does she ship the goods.

DIAGRAM
Wallet screen  -->  RPC helper  -->  BNB Smart Chain (the book)
     |                                    ^
     |                                    |
     +-------- explorer reads ------------+

Watch-only screen --> RPC helper --> book  (no keys, cannot send)

If screen and explorer disagree, believe the explorer.
If a screenshot and explorer disagree, believe the explorer.
If a delayed RPC and explorer disagree, wait; do not double-pay.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Network selector is part of the screen, not a sticker on the coins

MetaMask and similar apps have a network dropdown. If it says Ethereum, you are looking at Ethereum’s book. If it says BNB Smart Chain, you are looking at BSC. Add the wrong RPC and you may be looking at a **test network** or a fake chain that mimics names.

The same seed can have an address that **looks** the same on both (EVM chains share the 0x address format). The **balances are not shared**. A watch-only view of the Ethereum copy of your 0x will not show your BEP-20 Crystal Stones. That is not theft. That is the wrong book.

A delayed report on the right book is annoying. A perfect report on the wrong book is how people donate to a void. Check the dropdown every time you open the app to send or to declare yourself paid.

NOTE
Always check you are on the real explorer domain. Fake explorers exist. Bookmark BscScan the way you bookmark your bank. Never follow an explorer link from a random DM, and never install an “explorer app” from a sponsored message. Academy staff will not send you a special explorer “to verify your wallet,” and will not ask for remote desktop to “fix your RPC.”
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have a rule for disagreement: the book wins. You know that light wallets ask an RPC, that watch-only cannot spend, and that delayed reports are not frozen funds. Take the quiz. Then we open the vault combination — the seed phrase — slowly, as an operating manual, not as a dare.

## Say this out loud

- The app is a report. The chain is the book. When they disagree, the book wins.
- Light wallets ask an RPC. That is convenient and a trust trade. A delayed RPC is lag, not theft.
- Explorers read the book. Screenshots do not. Watch-only is a window without a pen.
- The network dropdown is which book you are reading. Same 0x shape is not a shared balance.
- Crystal Stones on BscScan means the published contract, not a clone with the same nickname.

Take the quiz. Then we open the vault combination — the seed phrase — slowly.

lessons.title: How a seed phrase is born
lessons.content:
# How a seed phrase is born

A **seed phrase** (also **recovery phrase** or **mnemonic**) is 12 or 24 ordinary words in a fixed order. It is not a slogan you invent. It is a human-readable encoding of a large random number.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say how those words are supposed to be born, why a website that “generates your seed” is a trap, and why you prove a restore with zero funds before you deposit anything you would miss.

Wallet software uses a standard most of the industry copied: **BIP-39**. BIP-39 is a recipe that turns random bits into words from a published list, then later turns those words back into keys. You do not need to implement it. You need the consequences: create the words in a place you trust, copy them exactly, treat any extra digital copy as a leak.

## Randomness is the whole product

When you tap “Create wallet,” the device is supposed to generate **entropy** — true-enough randomness — then map it onto a word list.

If the randomness is bad (a website generating your seed in a browser tab, a fake app, a “paper wallet generator” from 2017), an attacker may be able to regenerate the same words. The words will still look official. They will still restore in a real app. That is the point of the trap: the vault combination was born in the thief’s building.

**Rule:** create a seed **inside** a reputable wallet you installed from the official store, or on a hardware device’s own screen. Not inside Telegram. Not inside a Google Doc. Not on a website that says “generate seed.” Not on a laptop a cousin “already prepared for crypto.”

Entropy is the product because everything after it is mechanical. BIP-39 is public. The word list is public. Derivation is public. The only secret is the random number. If someone else chose that number, or if a weak generator chose it from a small set, the public recipe works for them too.

## Word order is the secret, not the poetry of the words

The same 12 words in a different order are a **different vault**. There is no “close enough.” There is no “I remember most of them.” There is no academy staff who can fill in the blanks.

The words come from a published list (2048 English words in the common list). That does **not** mean they are weak. The power is in the **combination and order**, like a long PIN made of dictionary words. A later lesson in this module unpacks the wordlist. Today: do not invent a memorable sentence. Invented phrases are guessable and not standard.

24 words is more entropy than 12. 12 is common and valid in BIP-39. Either must stay secret. Longer is not safer if you then photograph it. Shorter is not “beginner mode that the chain will forgive.”

TABLE
Myth | Fact | What people do after believing it
“I can pick words I will remember” | No. Invented phrases are guessable and not standard. | They write a proverb, get drained by a guesser, blame crypto
“24 words is always required” | 12 is common and valid in BIP-39. 24 is more entropy. Either must stay secret. | They refuse a good 12-word wallet and then screenshot a 24-word one
“I can skip three words I forgot” | No. Partial phrases are not a login hint. | They pay a “recovery agent” who wants the remaining words plus leftover funds
“The wallet company has a copy” | A real self-custody wallet must not. If they do, it is not self-custody. | They message support for a reset, then type the seed into a fake support site
“The academy can regenerate it from my student login” | Never. Your course account is not a vault. | They wait, then panic-send
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Alex sits in an internet café because his phone storage is full. A bookmark says “generate BIP-39 seed — free.”

1. The site shows 12 words. It also shows them to whoever runs the site.
2. Alex writes the words on a receipt, installs an official wallet at home, and restores. The balances will be visible to him — and to the generator.
3. He funds it with a practice amount “to see if it works.” It works. That is not a blessing.
4. Hours or weeks later the address empties. BscScan shows a signed send. The chain did its job.
5. The adult create path: official app or hardware screen, airplane mode if you like, pen ready, no café generator, no Telegram bot.

DIAGRAM
Entropy on the device you trust
        |
        v
BIP-39 words (12 or 24, ordered)
        |
        v
Master key  -->  many child keys  -->  addresses on each chain

If entropy is born on a stranger’s website, the stranger has the master key too.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Prove the birth before you fund the vault

Write the words **before** you put money in. Confirm the wallet can restore on a second view (the app usually asks you to tap the words in order). If you cannot restore with zero funds, do not fund it.

A create flow that skips the confirmation quiz is not “faster.” It is an untested backup. An untested backup is a rumour. Module 6 will make you do this as a lab. Today you need the rule: birth, write, confirm, then — maybe — a tiny receive.

Do not create a second wallet “for backup” by generating a second seed and mixing papers. One seed, one paper (or two copies of the same paper in two places), one restore proof. Extra unused seeds become extra ways to confuse yourself.

NOTE
Crystal Stones Academy will never generate a seed for you, never display your words in a student portal, and never ask you to paste them “so we can confirm BIP-39.” If a page uses our logo and a generate-or-paste box, it is theft. Close it. Report it. Do not type.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now know a seed is born as randomness on a device, not as a slogan in your head and not as a gift from a website. The next lesson is the tree those words grow: keys and addresses. You do not need a maths degree. You need to know why a restore can show zero without the coins being gone.

## Say this out loud

- A seed is generated randomness, not a password you chose and not a proverb you will remember.
- Create it in a real wallet or hardware screen, never on a website, never in a café generator, never in a chat bot.
- Order matters. Partial memory is not recovery. The academy cannot fill in blanks.
- Prove restore with zero funds before you deposit.
- 12 words can be valid. 24 words can be valid. A photographed phrase of either length is a leak.

Next: what those words turn into — keys and addresses — without a maths degree.

lessons.title: From words to keys to addresses
lessons.content:
# From words to keys to addresses

The seed is the root. Wallets grow a tree of keys from it so you can have many addresses without many pieces of paper.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to walk the stack — words, master key, child keys, public keys, address — and you should know why restoring the same words in a different app can show a zero balance without the coins having vanished.

You will hear **derivation path**. It is just a recipe: “from this seed, walk this folder structure, produce this key.” Different apps may use slightly different recipes. That is why restoring a seed in a **different brand** of wallet sometimes shows a **zero balance** even though the funds exist — the app is looking at a different branch of the tree.

## The stack, slowly

1. **Seed words** — human backup. 12 or 24 ordered words. This is what you write on paper.
2. **Master key** — the big secret derived from the words (and, if you used one, a passphrase — later lesson).
3. **Child private keys** — one per account or address the app creates. A **private key** is the number that can sign for one address.
4. **Public keys** — can be shown; used to check signatures. A public key is not an address, but an address is derived from it.
5. **Address** — the 0x… thing you publish to receive funds.

On BNB Smart Chain (an **EVM** chain — it speaks Ethereum’s style), addresses look like 0x plus 40 hex characters.

One seed can produce an Ethereum-style address, the **same looking** address on BSC, and different addresses if the derivation path or account index differs. Balances still live **per chain**. The format matching is convenience, not a shared piggy bank.

A **hex private key** is another way to export one child secret. If a site asks you to paste a hex key, that is the same family of disaster as pasting the seed. Sharing one child key can empty that address. Sharing the seed can empty the tree.

TABLE
You hold | You can share | You must not share | Typical mix-up
Seed words | Never | Never | “Support asked for 12 words to verify”
Private key (hex) | Never | Never | “Export key to connect faster”
Address | Yes, to receive | Sharing it does not let them spend | Thinking an address is a password
QR of the address | Yes, to receive | Check it is an address QR, not a seed QR | Scanning a “wallet QR” from a DM
Public key | Usually yes, still pointless for beginners | Not a seed, but do not scatter it into random forms | Thinking it is the vault
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Maya restores a MetaMask seed into Trust Wallet — both are examples of wallet apps, not a required pair. She expected Crystal Stones to appear. The app shows 0.

1. She does not panic-send, and she does not paste the seed into a third “checker” site.
2. She checks the network dropdown: is she on BNB Smart Chain (chain id 56), not Ethereum, not a testnet.
3. She checks whether she added the Crystal Stones contract 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. Adding is viewing. It is not a buy.
4. She opens BscScan on the address she **actually used** when she received funds — the address from the first app’s receive screen, not the address she assumes.
5. Possible honest reasons for a zero: wrong network, token not added, derivation account index is not account 0. Not a reason: “BSC deleted it.” Not a reason: “Trust Wallet ate MetaMask coins.”

DIAGRAM
12/24 words
    |
    v
master secret
    |
    +--> account 0 --> key --> 0xaaa...   (what most apps show first)
    +--> account 1 --> key --> 0xbbb...   (a different door, same seed)
    +--> other paths / other brands       (can look empty if you are on the wrong branch)

Same words, wrong folder of the tree, empty screen, funds still on the book.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why “one seed, many addresses” is power and a foot-gun

Apps show “Account 2,” “Add address,” “New wallet” inside the same seed. Those are often still the same tree. If you leak the seed, every account in that tree is in the race. Creating Account 2 is not a new backup. It is a new door with the same combination.

If you truly need a separate vault — household money versus a practice hot wallet — you need a **new seed**, a new paper, a new restore proof. Do not invent a “separate account” story that still sits on the leaked phrase.

Never type a seed into two random apps “to compare.” Each extra typing is an extra chance of malware. If you must restore, do it on a clean install from the official store, once. Module 6 will give you a lab version of that discipline.

NOTE
Never type a seed into two random apps “to compare.” Each extra typing is an extra chance of malware. If you must restore, do it on a clean install from the official store, once. Crystal Stones Academy will never ask you to paste a hex private key into a lesson, a mentor chat, or a “derivation checker.”
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now see the tree. Words are the root. Addresses are doors. Derivation is the hallway. The next lesson is the wordlist itself — why order matters mathematically enough for you to treat a shuffled paper as a different vault.

## Say this out loud

- Words become a master key, then child keys, then addresses. The paper is the root, not one door.
- Derivation path is which folder of that tree you are in. Wrong folder can look like a hack.
- Same 0x shape on BSC and Ethereum does not share balances.
- Explorer the address you used, not the address you assumed.
- A second account on the same seed is not a second backup. A leak of the words is a leak of the tree.

Next: BIP-39 wordlists and why order matters — the 2048-word list is public, the combination is not.

lessons.title: BIP-39 wordlists and why order matters
lessons.content:
# BIP-39 wordlists and why order matters

The BIP-39 English list is 2048 ordinary words. You can look it up. Looking it up does not open anyone’s vault. The secret is **which words, in which order, for this wallet**.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain why a shuffled paper is a different combination, why “I remember they were nature words” is not recovery, and why writing the numbers 1–12 next to the words is not optional decoration.

## The list is public on purpose

A recovery phrase has to be writable by a tired human with a pen. The designers picked a list of short, distinct words so that “apple” and “able” are less likely to collapse into the same scribble, and so that software can check that a word is even on the list.

**Checksum** means the last word is not fully free: it is partly determined by the earlier randomness, so a typo is more likely to be rejected. That is a kindness. It is not a backup of three forgotten words. If you are off by one word, the wallet should refuse. If you shuffle the first eleven and keep the twelfth, you do not have “almost the vault.” You have a failed checksum or a different vault.

People see the public list and think the system is weak. A PIN made of four digits is weak because there are 10,000 guesses. A BIP-39 12-word phrase is a combination from a 2048-word list, in order, with a checksum. Guessing it is not a hobby. Stealing a photo of it is.

## Order is the combination

Write the words numbered. Read them back in order, privately. If you copy them as a paragraph without numbers, a smudge or a line break will invent a new vault later.

The same twelve words, reversed, are not “your wallet backwards.” They derive a different master key. Software will often still accept them if they pass a checksum, and then show empty addresses. That empty screen is how people decide they were hacked when they only shuffled a page.

TABLE
What you did | What the software does | What you should do
Wrote 1–12, restored in order | Opens the original tree | Fund only after this works with zero
Shuffled the paper “to make it harder for a thief” | Opens a different tree, or fails checksum | Do not shuffle. Hide the paper. Do not encrypt it with a scheme you will forget
Skipped a word you thought was duplicate | Fails, or a different vault | Copy exactly. Duplicates can happen. Order still matters
Translated words into another language by hand | Not the same list | Use the list the wallet used. Do not translate
Picked twelve words from the public list because they were memorable | Guessable, non-standard entropy | Never invent. Let the device generate
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A shopkeeper, Riley, copies twelve words onto a card, then rewrites them alphabetically in a second notebook “so a thief cannot use the first card.”

1. The first card is the real combination, if it was copied in order.
2. The alphabetical notebook is a different order. Restoring from it will not show the funds.
3. A thief who finds the alphabetical notebook may still try orders, but Riley has mainly attacked herself: two papers, one of which will “fail” during a panic restore, at which point she may type both into a helper.
4. The adult move is two copies of the **same ordered list**, in two boring places, not two encodings.
5. If she already rewrote alphabetically and funded the wallet, she must still keep the ordered original. The sorted copy is not a backup. It is a puzzle.

DIAGRAM
Word 1 -> Word 2 -> ... -> Word 12   = vault A

Word 12 -> Word 11 -> ... -> Word 1 = vault B (different)
Alphabetical sort                    = vault C or a checksum fail

Public wordlist (2048 words)
        |
        v
Does NOT open vaults. Only the ordered pick does.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Languages, lookalikes, and “I will just remember”

Some wallets offer other BIP-39 language lists. Do not mix. If the device showed English, write English. Do not “translate for my auntie.” The auntie needs the exact words or she needs not to be the backup.

Lookalike handwriting is a practical enemy: l and i, r and n, words that differ by one letter on the list. Print in block letters. Leave space. Do not write on both sides of flimsy paper that will bleed.

Remembering twelve words in your head is a party trick until a hospital, a panic, or a year of disuse. This academy’s default is paper or steel, not memory. Memory is a single point of failure with no checksum.

NOTE
Do not invent a “coded” order as a security layer unless you can explain it to your future tired self at 3 a.m. Most people who shuffle, rotate, or translate their own backup lock themselves out more reliably than they lock out a thief. Hide the ordered paper. Do not encrypt it with folklore.
ENDNOTE


## Do not “improve” the list

People add extra words from their language, or replace a word that feels unlucky. That is a new vault the app will not confirm. People also write the words in two columns without numbers, then cannot remember whether they read down or across. Numbers exist so that panic has a sequence. Use them.

## What this lesson is for

You now treat order as the combination and the public list as a writing aid, not a weakness. Next is the physical job: writing and storing the words so you do not become a cautionary tale about photos, printers, and cloud folders.

## Say this out loud

- The BIP-39 list is public. The ordered pick is the secret.
- The same words in a new order are a different vault, or a checksum fail — not a clever lock.
- Number the lines 1–12 or 1–24. Copy exactly. Do not translate. Do not alphabetise.
- A checksum can catch a typo. It cannot reconstruct three forgotten words.
- Memory is not a backup. Paper with numbers is.

Next: writing and storing the words — paper, metal, never photos, never cloud.

lessons.title: Writing and storing the words
lessons.content:
# Writing and storing the words

This is the practical heart of self-custody. Cryptography does not save sloppy storage.

By the end of this lesson you should have a boring, adult plan: pen, numbered lines, a read-back, two locations if the amount would hurt, and zero photos. You should also know which “clever” hiding places are just delays before a disaster.

## How to write them

Use a pen, paper, or a purpose-made steel plate. Number the lines 1–12 or 1–24. Copy **exactly**. Then read them back once, out loud, privately. Do not correct “ugly handwriting” by taking a photo “to be sure.”

Do not type them into chat to “have a copy.” Do not email them. Do not put them in a tweet draft. Do not use a printer at an office — printers keep jobs. Do not type them into a notes app “until I buy a metal plate.” The temporary copy becomes the real copy.

Write in block letters. Do not write in pencil that will fade. Do not write on a sticky note that will travel on someone’s shoe. Do not write on the back of an identity photocopy. Theft of that envelope is identity plus vault.

If the wallet shows the words on screen, cover the screen from cameras, windows, and video calls. Finish writing. Confirm the in-app quiz. Then — and only then — consider a tiny receive. Crystal Stones Academy will never run a “backup verification” that requires you to type words into our site. If a site says that, it is theft.

## Where to put the paper

Good enough for practice amounts: a drawer that is not a postcard; not the same bag as the phone; not taped to the device.

Better for amounts you would miss: two copies in two places (flood in one house should not take both); steel if fire is a real risk; someone you trust **only** if you have thought about inheritance and theft by that person — this is a relationship decision, not a crypto trick. Module 5 returns to household and death. Today: do not put a seed in a family WhatsApp group “so everyone can help.”

A bank safe-deposit box can be a serious option for some adults. It has hours, paperwork, and a process. It is still more adult than Google Photos. It is not required for this course’s practice amounts.

TABLE
Place | Risk | When it is used anyway
Same phone case as the device | Stolen together | People want “convenience.” Convenience is the thief’s friend
Family WhatsApp group | Social and screenshot risk | “Backup by community.” Community is not a vault
Bank safe deposit | Process and access hours; sometimes a good option | Amounts you would miss, with a legal mind
Under a mattress only | Fire, theft, relatives | Folklore. Add a second location
Two boring locations | Usually the adult amateur setup | Practice this before you scale amounts
Photo “just for tonight” | Camera-roll backup, then forever | The most common self-own in this course
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A learner, Kemi, writes the words, funds a wallet with a test amount, then “improves” the backup by typing it into Notes.

1. She now has two backups: paper (good) and cloud (fatal).
2. The cloud one is the one that matters to an attacker. Account takeover, a stolen laptop, a curious roommate with her unlocked phone — any of these beats the locked drawer.
3. Deleting the note after it synced is not a time machine. Treat the seed as leaked if the copy existed long enough to leave the device.
4. Rotation, later in this module: new wallet, new paper, tiny test, move, retire.
5. If the note existed for thirty seconds on a phone that never backed up, she may still choose to rotate. Dignity is cheaper than a drained address.

DIAGRAM
Create wallet
    |
    v
Write words on numbered paper  -->  confirm restore with 0 funds
    |
    v
Tiny test receive on the right network
    |
    v
Only then: larger amount, if ever
    |
    v
Never: photo, cloud, printer, group chat
ENDDIAGRAM

## Steel, fire, and the urge to get fancy

Steel plates exist so that a house fire does not eat the combination. They are examples of a tool, not a shopping list for week one of Basic. If your practice amount is smaller than the plate, paper in two dry places is enough. If you later hold an amount a fire would ruin you for, steel becomes a conversation, not a personality.

Do not stamp a seed into a decorative object you will photograph for Instagram. Do not engrave it on jewellery you wear to a market. Physical backup means **boring and unadvertised**.

NOTE
Crystal Stones Academy will never run a “backup verification” that requires you to type words into our site. If a site says that, it is theft. We will also never ask you to upload a photo of the paper “for your student record.” Official stores, official apps, your paper, your drawer.
ENDNOTE


## Ink, time, and the urge to type

If your hand is shaking, slow down. A wrong word written neatly is a wrong vault. A right word written so badly you will read “sword” as “word” is also a wrong vault. Block letters. Numbered lines. One private read-back. The five minutes you save by photographing the screen are the five minutes a camera-roll backup uses to leave the house.

## What this lesson is for

You have a write-and-store ritual. Next is an optional extra secret — the passphrase, the so-called 25th word — and why most beginners should leave it off until they can teach it.

## Say this out loud

- Ink and steel beat cloud. Numbered paper beats a paragraph. A read-back beats a photo.
- Two locations beat one clever hiding place. The same bag as the phone is one location.
- Confirm restore before funding. An untested paper is a rumour.
- A digital copy poisons the setup. If it synced, rotate.
- Do not print, do not chat, do not decorate, do not file the seed with your passport photocopy.

Next: the optional extra word — passphrase — and why most beginners should leave it off.

lessons.title: The optional passphrase (25th word) — power and how people lock themselves out
lessons.content:
# The optional passphrase (25th word) — power and how people lock themselves out

Some wallets let you add a **passphrase** on top of the 12/24 words. People call it a 25th word. It is not on the sticker. You invent it.

Technically it derives a **different** vault from the same words. Same paper, different extra secret → different addresses. That is power. It is also how careful people lock themselves out more thoroughly than a thief ever could.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what a passphrase does, why this academy’s default for Basic is **off**, and what a zero balance after a restore might mean if you ever turned it on.

## Why it exists

If someone finds the paper, they still need the passphrase. It is a second factor **you must remember** (or store as carefully as the seed, which means you now have two secrets).

It is used by people who want a **decoy**: the twelve words alone open an empty or small wallet; the twelve words plus passphrase open the real one. That is an advanced household and duress design. It fails if you forget which is which, if you tell the wrong story under stress, or if you never wrote the passphrase because you thought the device PIN was the passphrase.

## Why beginners lock themselves out

They turn it on without writing it. They think the PIN is the passphrase. They type a space or a capital letter once and never again. They enable it on one app and restore in another app without it, see a zero balance, and panic-send. They use “Family2024” or a birthday, which is a second factor a cousin can guess.

A passphrase is **case-sensitive** and space-sensitive. “Family 2024” and “Family2024” and “family2024” are three different vaults. There is no “forgot passphrase” email. There is no academy reset. The paper seed will still “work.” It will open the un-passphrased tree. That tree can be empty. The funds are in the hidden tree you cannot open.

TABLE
If you | Result | Academy default
Do not understand this lesson | Leave passphrase OFF | Yes
Use it | Treat it as seriously as the seed; two secrets now | Only after you can teach this lesson
Forget it | The paper seed opens an empty decoy wallet. Funds are in the hidden one you cannot open | Avoid
Confuse it with the device PIN | PIN still only locks furniture. Passphrase changes the vault | Name the object
Use a birthday | Guessable second factor | Do not
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A user, Sola, enables a passphrase “Family2024” then restores on a new phone without it.

1. The familiar 12 words work. Balance is 0.
2. Sola assumes a hack. She is looking at the **un-passphrased** tree.
3. The funds are still in the passphrased tree — which she also might have forgotten, including whether it was “Family2024” or “family2024”.
4. If she now creates a brand new seed and moves nothing, she has not healed anything. If she types the old words plus guesses into a “recovery helper,” she has donated the vault.
5. If she still remembers the exact passphrase, she restores with words **plus** that exact string, then checks BscScan on the address that actually held funds.

DIAGRAM
12/24 words alone     -->  vault A (often empty if you used a passphrase)
12/24 words + "X"     -->  vault B
12/24 words + "x"     -->  vault C (different)

PIN / fingerprint     -->  still just this device
ENDDIAGRAM

## Leave it off until you can teach it

This academy’s default advice for Basic: **leave the passphrase off** until you can explain it to someone else without notes. Complexity is not safety if you are the one who fails the puzzle.

Hardware wallets make passphrases easy to enable and easy to forget. Software wallets hide the setting under “advanced.” If you did not intend to create a hidden wallet, do not poke advanced settings while tired. If you already did, write the exact passphrase as carefully as the seed — then admit you now have two objects to inherit, lose, or leak.

A passphrase is not a substitute for a steel plate. It is not a substitute for avoiding screenshots. It is an extra derivation input. Treat it that way, or leave it off.

NOTE
This academy’s default advice for Basic: leave the passphrase off until you can explain it to someone else without notes. We will never ask you for a 25th word, a PIN, or a “hidden wallet check.” If a helper wants those, they want the vault.
ENDNOTE


## Hidden wallets and fake support

Some thieves ask you to “open the hidden wallet” and will coach you through enabling a passphrase on a seed they already stole, or on words they want you to type. You do not need a hidden wallet to finish Basic. You need a paper you can restore.

If a helper says the 25th word is your date of birth “for inheritance,” they are guessing a vault they hope you already made. Do not confirm or deny secrets on a call. Hang up. Open the official app from the icon you installed. Not from their link.

## What this lesson is for

You can now refuse a feature that would make you safer on paper and poorer in practice. Next is the leak: what to do when you think the words got out, including the race you do not win by hoping.

## Say this out loud

- A passphrase makes a different wallet from the same words. It is optional. Off is valid.
- Forgetting it is as final as losing the seed. The paper will still open an empty decoy.
- PIN is not the passphrase. Birthday is not a passphrase. A space and a capital letter matter.
- A zero after restore might mean wrong network, wrong derivation — or a passphrase you forgot to type.
- Do not turn it on to feel advanced. Turn it on when you can teach it and store it.

Next: the leak. What to do when you think the words got out.

lessons.title: If you think the seed leaked
lessons.content:
# If you think the seed leaked

Assume spent. Not “maybe later.” Spent.

A leak is: photo, cloud sync, screen share, typing into a website, a stranger who “helps you restore,” a repair-shop backup, a Discord “support” form, a remote-desktop session that watched the words, a 2FA code you handed to someone who then opened your email and your cloud photos.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to run **rotation** without a helper, and you should be able to name which secret leaked — seed, exchange password, or device PIN — because those are three different playbooks.

## Rotation, not hope

1. On a device you trust, create a **new** wallet (new words). Write those words properly, numbered, no photo.
2. Confirm restore of the **new** wallet with zero funds.
3. From the **old** wallet, send a **tiny test** to the new address on the **correct network** (BNB Smart Chain for BEP-20 assets in this academy).
4. Confirm on BscScan.
5. Move the rest. Leave a little BNB in the old address only if you still need to move tokens; then move those; then stop.
6. Stop using the old wallet. Treat old words as radioactive. Do not “keep it for small stuff.”

Do not wait “to see if they take it.” Bots watch. Humans delay. A balance still showing is not safety. It is a countdown you cannot see.

Do not send everything in one first try to a mistyped address. That is how people donate a leak to a void. Test, explorer, remainder.

Do not ask a helper to “check the seed.” They check it into their wallet.

TABLE
Bad move | Why | Do this instead
Leaving funds in the old wallet | The leak is a race you will lose | New wallet, test, move, retire
Sending everything in one first try to a mistyped address | You can donate to a void | Tiny test, BscScan, then remainder
Asking a helper to “check the seed” | They check it into their wallet | You restore on an official app you installed
Changing only the PIN | PIN is furniture | Rotation of the seed
Posting “I was hacked, here is my address, send gas” | Predators will answer | Get BNB from a venue you chose, not a stranger
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** You pasted 12 words into a “wallet connect” site. You still see the balance.

1. That does not mean you are safe. The site may already have the combination and be waiting, or a bot may be watching the address.
2. Create the new wallet now, on the official app, paper ready.
3. Prove restore of the new words with zero funds.
4. Move a tiny BNB test on BNB Smart Chain. Confirm on BscScan that it landed on **your** new address.
5. Move remaining BNB and tokens (Crystal Stones only if you already held them — this is not a buy order). Then retire the old words. Speed matters more than dignity.

DIAGRAM
Old wallet (compromised)
        |
        |  tiny test  -->  explorer confirms new door
        |  then remainder (tokens need BNB gas)
        v
New wallet (fresh words, clean backup)
        |
        v
Old words = radioactive. Do not reuse. Do not “check” with support.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Name which secret leaked

If the leak was an **exchange password**, that is a different playbook: change password, revoke sessions, 2FA, contact the exchange. That is **not** a seed rotation. If the leak was a **device PIN**, lock the furniture; it does not move the book by itself. If the leak was a **seed**, rotate. If you are not sure which leaked, assume the seed if the words were ever typed, photographed, or shown on a call.

“Support asked for 12 words” is always a leak if you complied — whether they used the academy’s name, Binance’s name, Trust Wallet’s name, or MetaMask’s name. Those companies, and this academy, do not need the words. A human who asks is not confused. They are collecting.

Never send leftover funds to a stranger who promises to “reverse the hack” or “trace the mixer.” That is a second theft. This academy will not give recovery-agent advice that requires sending leftover funds to a stranger.

NOTE
If the leak was an exchange password, that is a different playbook: change password, revoke sessions, 2FA, contact the exchange. That is not a seed rotation. Name which secret leaked. Academy staff will never ask you to paste old words “so we can freeze the chain.” The chain does not freeze for our course login.
ENDNOTE


## What “leaked” includes, said plainly

A screen share while the words were visible. A repair shop that backed up the phone. A photo you deleted after iCloud already had it. A “wallet connect” form. A cousin who helped you type. A printer. A password-manager share with a teammate. A 2FA code you handed over that opened the email that opened the photos.

If you are arguing with yourself about whether it counts, it counts. Rotation is cheaper than a paragraph of hope.

## Do not pay a recovery agent

Someone will offer to “trace” the thief if you send remaining coins to their address, or if you share the old words so they can “front-run.” That is a second thief. This academy will not give recovery-agent advice that requires sending leftover funds to a stranger. Rotate to a vault they do not have. That is the whole honest move.

## What this lesson is for

You have a leak playbook. Take the quiz. Then we practise addresses, networks, and receiving without theatre — the public door, not the combination.

## Say this out loud

- Leaked seed means new wallet, test, move, retire. Balance still showing is not safety.
- Never “verify” a seed with a helper, a website, or a remote-desktop technician.
- Exchange password leaks are not seed leaks. PIN leaks are not seed leaks. Name the object.
- Tiny test on the correct network, then explorer, then remainder. Do not donate to a mistype.
- Support that asks for 12 words is theft, even when it uses a logo you trust.

Take the quiz. Then we practise addresses, networks, and receiving without theatre.
