lessons.title: What an address is (and is not)
lessons.content:
# What an address is (and is not)

An **address** is the public door. On BNB Smart Chain it looks like 0x followed by 40 hexadecimal characters (0–9 and a–f, sometimes mixed with A–F).

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what an address is, what it is not, why you copy-paste instead of dictating, and why a token contract is a different door from a person’s wallet.

It is not a bank account with a name on file at a branch. It is not something you can “reset” if you paste it wrong. It is not proof of who a person is. It is not a Crystal Stones account number issued by the academy. Anyone can generate an address. Anyone can send to it. Only the matching key can send **from** it.

## A door, not an identity, not a customer record

When you give someone an address, you are giving them a public identifier the chain can credit. You are not giving them permission to know your legal name. You are not opening a file at Crystal Stones Academy. You are not creating a reversible bank transfer.

If you send to the wrong door, the network does not call you. If you send to the right door on the wrong chain, the network you used is happy and the network you meant never hears about it. The next lesson forces the full sentence: asset, network, standard, address. Today, own the door.

Reuse of addresses is common on EVM chains. Privacy is imperfect. Treat an address as public the moment you share it: it can be watched on BscScan by anyone. That is not a reason to hide your receiving address from a client who must pay you. It is a reason not to also paste your seed beside it.

## Checksum: the mixed-case hint

Many EVM wallets show addresses with **mixed capital letters**. That is a **checksum** — extra information so a typo is more likely to look invalid. If you lower-case everything, some checks go away. Prefer copy-paste over retyping. Then check the **first 6 and last 6** characters on the screen you will send from.

Dictating an address on a phone call is how two characters get swapped. The send can still look “valid enough.” Funds go to a door nobody you know can open — or to a stranger. Copy-paste exists. Use it. Then still check the ends. Clipboard malware, later in this module, is why the last check is not paranoia.

TABLE
Safe habit | Unsafe habit | Why the unsafe one survives
Copy from the wallet receive screen | Retype from memory | Pride. Memory is not 40 hex characters
Check first 6 and last 6 | Glance at “0x” and send | Speed. Thieves also like speed
Use the explorer to confirm a past receive | Trust a screenshot someone DMed | Politeness. Politeness is not a row on BscScan
Give one address you control | Give an address a stranger generated “for you” | Helpfulness. Helpfulness can be a redirection
Treat contract and wallet as different doors | Send BNB to the token contract as if it were a friend | The 0x prefix looks the same
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Jordan dictates his BSC address to a client on a noisy call. Two characters get swapped.

1. The client sends USDT as BEP-20 to the swapped door. The wallet may even show the address as valid.
2. BscScan shows a successful send — to someone else, or to an empty key.
3. Jordan’s receive screen never changes. He argues. The book already moved.
4. The adult path: he copies from the receive screen, pastes into the chat, then reads first 6 and last 6 aloud while looking at his own screen. The client does the same before confirming.
5. If the amount would hurt, they do a tiny test first. That ritual belongs to the whole module. It starts with not dictating.

DIAGRAM
Person’s wallet address   -->  they can spend what they receive
Token contract address    -->  the program that defines the token
You receive tokens at the person’s address, recorded by the program.

Academy printing a contract  =  verify / add token
Academy printing a contract  !=  “send funds here”
ENDDIAGRAM

## Contracts are addresses too

A **token contract** is also an 0x address, but it is a **program**, not a person’s door. Crystal Stones’ token contract is a program that keeps a list of who holds how many tokens. The published contract is 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00.

Sending BNB to the **token contract** by mistake is not the same as sending Crystal Stones to **your friend’s wallet**. Different doors, different results. Beginners mix “the token’s contract” with “the person’s address” because both start with 0x and both appear on BscScan.

When we print Crystal Stones’ contract, that is so you can **add/verify the token** in a wallet or explorer. It is not a deposit address for the academy. It is not a buy order. It is not a tuition wallet. Paid tracks, when live, use a checkout rail — USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout — not this contract as a piggy bank.

A contract can also be a **spender** you approve later in this course. Seeing 0x should make you ask: whose door, or which program? If you cannot answer, do not send.

NOTE
When we print Crystal Stones’ contract 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00, that is so you can add or verify the token in a wallet or explorer. It is not a deposit address for the academy, not a salary wallet, and not a place to send BNB “to activate Crystal Stones.”
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have a public door you can share and a contract you must not confuse with that door. Next you will glue three more words onto every send: asset, network, standard. Nicknames without roads are how USDT disappears.

## Say this out loud

- Address means public door. Key means who can leave. Sharing the door does not share the key.
- Copy, then check first and last 6. Do not dictate forty hex characters on a call.
- Token contract is not a friend’s wallet. Both can look like 0x.
- Academy contract printouts are not payment addresses and not a buy order.
- A successful send on BscScan to the wrong door is still the wrong door.

Next: networks — the most expensive beginner mix-up. Asset, network, standard — say all three.

lessons.title: Asset, network, standard — say all three
lessons.content:
# Asset, network, standard — say all three

You already met this in Crypto Foundations. This course makes it muscle memory, because wallets will let you sign a disaster in two taps.

Always speak a send as a full sentence: **I am sending [asset] on [network] as [standard] to [address].**

By the end of this lesson that sentence should feel as automatic as saying a bank name plus an account number. “I’ll just send USDT” is how funds vanish while both people are honest.

## Nicknames are not roads

Examples of full sentences:

- I am sending **USDT** on **BNB Smart Chain** as **BEP-20** to 0xabc...
- I am sending **BNB** (native coin) on **BNB Smart Chain** to 0xabc...
- I am sending **USDT** on **Tron** as **TRC-20** to a T-address
- I am sending **USDT** on **Ethereum** as **ERC-20** to 0xabc...

USDT is a **nickname**. The nickname appears on several roads. The roads do not share the money. **ERC-20** is a token standard on Ethereum. **BEP-20** is a token standard on BNB Smart Chain. **TRC-20** is a token standard on Tron. Same ticker letters. Different books. Different address shapes (0x versus T…).

A wallet that can hold all three will still let you pick the wrong one. The app is a translator. It will not parent you. The receive screen on an exchange will usually name the network in small text. Read the small text. If it says BEP-20, do not send TRC-20 because “USDT is USDT.”

TABLE
Nickname | Common roads | Address look | What happens if you mix them
USDT | Ethereum (ERC-20), BSC (BEP-20), Tron (TRC-20), others | 0x on EVM; T… on Tron | Often irrecoverable for a beginner
BNB | BNB Smart Chain (native), also wrapped forms | 0x on BSC | Wrapped BNB is not the native gas coin
Crystal Stones | BNB Smart Chain BEP-20 (the official story) | 0x contract + 0x wallets | A clone on another chain is a different token
Bitcoin | Bitcoin | bc1… / 1… / 3… (not 0x) | Sending BTC to 0x is the wrong planet
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario — the academy checkout warning.** Paid tracks, when live, ask for **USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20)** and warn: sending on another network may mean loss.

1. Sam has USDT on Tron (TRC-20) in an exchange account. She sees “USDT” and sends to a BEP-20 checkout address.
2. The letters still say USDT. The receiver’s BSC book never credits them.
3. Support may or may not be able to help; this academy will not promise a rescue. The warning exists because this mistake is common and ugly.
4. The adult path: she withdraws or converts so that the asset, network, and standard match the invoice sentence, then sends a tiny test if the rail allows, then the rest.
5. She never “tries another network” with the same amount hoping one of them will land.

DIAGRAM
Wrong: “I’ll just send USDT”

Right:
  Asset: USDT
  Network: BNB Smart Chain
  Standard: BEP-20
  To: 0x… (checked, first 6 and last 6)
  Gas: small BNB on that same wallet
  Chain id: 56
ENDDIAGRAM

## Native coin versus token

On BSC:

- **BNB** is the native coin. It pays **gas**. It is not a BEP-20 contract you add.
- **Crystal Stones** is a BEP-20 **token**. The contract keeps balances. Moving it still costs **BNB** gas.

If you have tokens and 0 BNB, you can be “rich” on screen and unable to move. Scammers will offer to “unlock gas” if you pay them first. That is theft. Get a little BNB from a venue you chose — never a stranger’s invoice.

This academy does not tell you to buy Crystal Stones to complete Basic. Adding a token contract to a wallet is **viewing**, not investing. The public contract to verify is 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. Verify, do not treat as a deposit address.

A full sentence also names **from which kind of account**: exchange IOU versus self-custody address. Withdrawing from an exchange to “BEP-20” when you meant “ERC-20” is the same class of error as a wallet-to-wallet mix-up. The dropdown on the exchange is a network selector too.

NOTE
This academy does not tell you to buy Crystal Stones to complete Basic. Adding a token contract to a wallet is viewing, not investing. Checkout warnings about BEP-20 exist because sending the same ticker on another network can result in loss — not because we need you to hold a project token.
ENDNOTE


## Why the wallet will not save you

The send button does not know your intent. If USDT BEP-20 and a Tron USDT are both on the phone, the wrong tap is a valid instruction on the wrong book. Valid is not correct. Explorers will show success. Success is not “arrived where I meant.”

Say the sentence out loud before you tap, even if you feel silly. Silly is cheaper than a support ticket that cannot reprint the coins. If the other person cannot say the sentence, stop. Two confused adults do not make a network.

## What this lesson is for

You now have the sentence that prevents the ugliest beginner loss. Next is receiving without getting hunted: new address habits, memos on centralised exchanges, QR codes that are not magic truth.

## Say this out loud

- Nickname is not the road. USDT on the wrong chain is a different object.
- Always say asset, network, and standard together, then the address, then who pays gas.
- BNB pays BSC gas. Tokens do not pay the courier. A zero-BNB wallet full of tokens is stuck.
- Checkout warnings about BEP-20 exist because this mistake is common and ugly.
- Crystal Stones, as taught here, is a BEP-20 token on BNB Smart Chain — verify the contract, do not send to it as if it were a person.

Next: how to receive without getting hunted — new address, memo/tag on a CEX, QR.

lessons.title: How to receive without getting hunted
lessons.content:
# How to receive without getting hunted

Receiving looks easy. That is why people get sloppy.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to run a clean receive on BNB Smart Chain, know when an exchange needs a **memo** or **tag**, and treat QR codes as data that can lie.

## The clean receive

1. Open **your** wallet, official app — Trust Wallet or MetaMask as examples of wallet apps, not as required brands.
2. Select the **network** (BNB Smart Chain for Crystal Stones / BEP-20 USDT). Confirm chain id 56 if the app shows it.
3. Tap Receive. Copy the address or show the QR **from that screen**.
4. Send a **tiny test** from the other side first if the amount matters.
5. Confirm on BscScan, then send the rest.

Never reuse a “receive address” someone else generated “for you” in a DM. Generate from your app. A helpful stranger who builds the invoice PDF with a QR can swap the door. Your receive screen is the source. Their PDF is a copy that can be poisoned.

If you are receiving onto a **centralised exchange** (a custodial account), read their deposit page until you can say asset, network, standard, address, and whether a **memo/tag/payment ID** is required. A memo is an extra number some exchanges use to credit the right customer, because many customers deposit to one shared chain address. Missing memo on those rails can mean a delay or a painful support ticket. BNB Smart Chain personal wallets usually do **not** use memos. Do not invent a memo for a self-custody 0x.

## QR codes are not magic truth

A QR can encode your address (good), a whole payment request (amount + address), a malicious URL, or in nightmare cases, something you should not scan with a seed-aware camera app.

Scan wallet QRs with the wallet, not with a random “crypto scanner” from an ad. After scan, read the address on the confirm sheet — first 6 and last 6 — as if you had pasted. The QR did not bless the digits.

A printed QR on a shop counter should match the watch-only tablet or the receive screen behind the counter. If they disagree, stop. The counter is a report. The receive screen or explorer is closer to the book.

## Clipboard malware

Some malware waits until you copy an 0x address, then **replaces** it with the thief’s address. You paste without looking. You send.

Habit: after paste, check first 6 and last 6 **on the sending screen** before you hit confirm. Every time. Especially on a computer. A phone is not immune. Speed is the malware’s friend.

TABLE
Step | Why | Skip it and you get
Tiny test | Proves door + network before the amount that hurts | A beautiful, irreversible mistake
Explorer confirm | Book, not screenshot | A JPEG argument
Check ends after paste | Beats clipboard malware | A send to a hunter who watches busy addresses
Official app receive screen | Beats a PDF invoice with a swapped QR | Paying a stranger who designed the invoice
Read memo rules on a CEX deposit | Shared addresses need a tag | A deposit the exchange cannot auto-credit
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** You copy your address from Trust Wallet to tell a client. On the laptop, malware swaps it.

1. The client pastes and pays without checking ends.
2. Explorer shows a send to an address that is not yours.
3. The client “did everything right” except the check of the ends. Both of you now have a problem the chain will not reverse.
4. Prevention is dull: you paste into the chat, then read first 6 and last 6 from your receive screen while the client reads the same digits from their send screen.
5. For a large invoice, the tiny test is cheaper than a lawyer.

DIAGRAM
Your receive screen --> copy/QR
        |
        v
Sender pastes --> checks first/last 6 --> tiny tx
        |
        v
Explorer shows it on the right book
        |
        v
Remainder

If a CEX is the receiver: address + memo/tag as the deposit page states.
ENDDIAGRAM

## New address, old address, hunter’s address

On Bitcoin, people often generate a fresh address per receive. On BSC, reuse is common. Hunters still watch busy addresses and sometimes send **dust** — tiny token amounts — to bait you into a draining site. You do not have to rotate addresses every invoice. You do have to ignore mystery tokens and not click “claim.”

A hunter’s address can also land in your **address book** after one paste. The next lesson on poisoned books goes deeper. Today: after every paste, check ends. Do not trust last-used.

NOTE
Never reuse a receive address someone else generated “for you” in a DM. Generate from your app. Academy staff will not send you a special QR to “activate receiving,” and will not ask for remote desktop to “fix a memo.”
ENDNOTE


## Reuse versus rotation, as a shop habit

You may reuse one BSC address for a stall. Hunters can watch it. That does not force a new seed every morning. It does force: ignore dust, ignore claim links, check ends every send, and do not put the seed on the stall tablet. A busy public address is a visible door. Keep the combination off the street.

## What this lesson is for

You can receive like an adult: your screen, the right network, a test, an explorer row, a memo when a CEX actually requires one. Next: adding a token is not buying it — Crystal Stones’ contract as a verify-only drill.

## Say this out loud

- Receive from your app’s network-correct screen. Do not let a DM generate your door.
- Test, explorer, then remainder. Check ends after every paste.
- Random QRs are not addresses until proven. Scan with the wallet, then still read the digits.
- Some exchange deposits need a memo or tag. Personal BSC wallets usually do not. Do not invent one. Do not skip one when the deposit page requires it.
- Mystery dust is bait. Receiving it is not a request to tap Claim.

Next: adding Crystal Stones as a token view — contract verification, not a purchase.

lessons.title: Adding a token is not buying it
lessons.content:
# Adding a token is not buying it

Wallets show native coins automatically. They do **not** magically know every BEP-20 token. You **add** a token by pointing at its **contract**. That only **displays** a balance. It does not purchase anything.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to add Crystal Stones as a view on BNB Smart Chain using the published contract, and you should treat a mystery airdrop as bait rather than a gift.

This academy shows the official contract so you can recognise fakes. It is not an order to buy, hold, or add liquidity. You can finish this course with an empty wallet. Empty and competent beats funded and confused.

## How to add without a trap

1. Get the contract from a source you already trust **and** from a second source (project site + explorer search — not a Telegram screenshot alone).
2. For Crystal Stones, the published BEP-20 contract is 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00.
3. In the wallet, on **BNB Smart Chain** (chain id 56), choose Add token / custom token and paste.
4. Confirm the **name/symbol** the contract reports. Clones often mimic the name.
5. If a stranger sends you a “token” you never added, **do not tap it** to “claim.” That is a common scam path (a dust airdrop that opens a draining site).

Adding a token does not move coins. It does not require Approve. If the add-token sheet suddenly asks you to sign Approve, you are no longer adding a view. You are in Module 4’s danger zone. Reject.

If after adding you still see 0, you may simply hold 0. That is allowed. It may also mean you are on the wrong network, or you pasted a clone. Check BscScan for **your address** plus **that contract**. The book wins.

TABLE
Healthy | Unhealthy | What the unhealthy one is selling
Add contract you verified on BscScan | Add whatever a pop-up said you received | A draining site behind a familiar name
View zero balance after adding | Panic-buy because the logo appeared | A buy order dressed as a tutorial
Ignore unknown airdrops | Connect wallet to “activate” a mystery token | Your Approve signature
Paste 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 on BSC | Paste a lookalike contract from a sponsored Google result | A clone
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A wallet shows “Crystal Stones” after a random airdrop. The contract is **not** 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00.

1. It is a clone. Tapping it opens a site that asks you to approve unlimited spending.
2. You approve. The clone did not make you rich. It rented your signature.
3. Later, real tokens you actually held can leave. BscScan will show you authorised a spender.
4. The adult path: hide or ignore the mystery token. Do not swap it. Do not “claim.” If you want the real Crystal Stones **view**, add the published contract yourself, on BSC, as a display.
5. Still not a buy order. Viewing zero is a successful lab.

DIAGRAM
Verified contract  -->  add to wallet on BSC  -->  view only
Unknown airdrop    -->  ignore                -->  do not approve

Name match is not contract match.
Logo match is not contract match.
Telegram screenshot is not a second source.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What BscScan shows when you did it right

Open the published contract on BscScan. You should see a token page, holders, and transfers. Your address, if you hold any, appears in that list. If you hold none, you will not appear. That is not a bug.

Read the contract address character by character against what you pasted — at least first 6 and last 6, preferably more. Lookalike contracts change the middle. Hunters count on fatigue.

This academy will not invent yield, listing dates, or mineral-vault proof. Crystal Stones’ RWA story is **their claim to verify**. Adding the contract does not verify a mine. It verifies which program your wallet is counting.

NOTE
This academy shows the official contract so you can recognise fakes. It is not an order to buy, hold, or add liquidity. Paid-track checkout, when you meet it, is USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout — not Crystal Stones token, and not this contract as a tuition address.
ENDNOTE


## Decimals, symbols, and other costume jewellery

A clone can copy the name, the logo, and even the **decimals** (how many fraction digits the token uses). None of that is the contract. The contract is the 0x. If BscScan’s token page for your pasted address is not 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00, you added a different program.

Some wallets search by name. Searching “Crystal Stones” can return a list of lookalikes. Do not pick the first logo. Paste the string. If the search result’s contract differs in the middle, it is not a checksum variant. It is a different door.

A zero view after a correct add means you hold zero. That is a complete lab. It is not a prompt to visit a DEX. It is not a prompt to message an admin for an airdrop.

## What this lesson is for

You can add a token as a view and you can refuse a clone. Next: QR codes, lookalike characters, and poisoned address books — the last receiving traps before we send.

## Say this out loud

- Adding a token means viewing a contract’s balances. It is not a purchase and not an approval.
- Verify the contract twice. For Crystal Stones, match 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 on BNB Smart Chain.
- Mystery airdrops are bait. Name match is not contract match.
- A zero after adding can be honest. Check the book before you chase a claim site.
- Never send BNB to a contract “to activate” a token. That story is theft.

Next: QR codes, lookalike characters, and poisoned address books.

lessons.title: QR codes, lookalike characters, and poisoned address books
lessons.content:
# QR codes, lookalike characters, and poisoned address books

Hunters do not always need your seed. Sometimes they only need you to send to a door that **looks like** a door you already trust.

By the end of this lesson you should treat address books, recent-send lists, and QR stickers as reports that can be poisoned, and you should check first 6 and last 6 even when the name in the book says “Sam.”

## Poisoned address books

You send to a client once. The wallet saves the address under a name. Later, malware or a clipboard swap inserts a **lookalike** into the book, or you yourself paste a hunter’s address once and the book keeps it as “Sam.”

**Lookalike characters** in hex are limited, but hunters still pick addresses that share the same first 4–6 and last 4–6 as a busy victim or a famous wallet. Your eyes love the ends. They skip the middle. Check more than a glance. For a large send, compare the full string to a source you already trust — a previous BscScan receive, not a Telegram “updated wallet.”

Some scams **poison** public labels: they send a tiny amount from an address they control to your address, hoping your wallet’s “recent” list will make their address look familiar. Familiar is not verified. Recent is not a checksum.

TABLE
What you trusted | How it lies | Adult check
Address book name “Sam” | The name is local; the 0x can change | First 6 and last 6 against Sam's last known good, or a tiny test
QR sticker on a counter | Sticker can be swapped overnight | Match the shop’s receive screen or watch-only tablet
Recent send list | A dust sender wants to look like a friend | Do not send back to mystery dust
Looks like first and last 6 | Hunters grind for vanity ends | Read more of the middle, or compare full string
A PDF invoice QR | Designer or a forwarder can swap it | Generate from your own receive screen if you are the payee; if you are the payer, confirm with the payee out of band
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A shop, Mallam Yusuf’s stall in Suleja, prints a QR for BEP-20 USDT. A visitor swaps the paper QR when the stall is busy.

1. Customers pay. BscScan shows success. Yusuf’s wallet does not move.
2. He was paid to the hunter’s door. The chain is not confused. The sticker was.
3. The fix is operational: the QR lives on a screen he controls, or he checks the stall QR against his receive screen every morning — first 6 and last 6.
4. He does not then type his seed into a “QR recovery” app a customer recommends.
5. If a day’s takings matter, a watch-only tablet showing incoming BscScan rows is more honest than a paper square that can walk.

DIAGRAM
Good payee flow

  Receive screen (source of truth)
        |
        v
  QR shown from that screen
        |
        v
  Payer scans --> reads ends on confirm sheet --> tiny test if it hurts
        |
        v
  Explorer row on payee’s address

Poisoned flow

  Old QR / saved “Sam” / dust “recent”
        |
        v
  Payer trusts the label
        |
        v
  Book credits a hunter
ENDDIAGRAM

## Homoglyphs, handwriting, and “I’ll type it”

You will not usually type a 0x by hand. If you do, you will lose. If someone sends an address as an image, retype nothing — ask for a copy-paste and still check ends, or better, confirm a tiny test.

On EVM, mixed-case checksums exist to catch typos. A QR can still encode a perfectly checksummed wrong door. Checksum is not “this is my friend.” Checksum is “this string is internally consistent.”

If you maintain an address book, treat edits as a security event. A cousin with your unlocked phone can change Sam to a hunter. A shared family phone is a shared address book. Module 5 talks about household sharing without sharing a seed. Today: do not let the book be the only copy of a destination.

NOTE
Confirm destinations the way you confirm a bank account: out of band, on a channel you already trust, plus a tiny test when the amount would hurt. Academy staff will not send you a “new official address” in a DM. We will not ask you to update your address book from a WhatsApp broadcast.
ENDNOTE


## Out-of-band means a second channel you already trust

If Sam's address arrives in Telegram, confirm a first-6 last-6 on a phone call you know is Sam, or on a channel you have used for a year. Do not confirm on a second Telegram account that popped up. Hunters occupy both seats.

For a shop, the second channel can be the receive screen behind the counter, not a second sticker. For an exchange withdrawal, the second channel is the exchange’s own deposit page, not a DM that “updated the wallet.”

Write one trusted destination on paper if you send to it often — Sam's full 0x in your own handwriting, stored with household papers, not with the seed. Then the address book is a convenience you still check, not the only copy.

## What this lesson is for

You now treat labels, stickers, and recents as untrusted until checked. Take the quiz. Then we send: gas, approvals, and the loaded gun called Approve.

## Say this out loud

- An address-book name is a sticker you wrote. It can be wrong. Check the 0x.
- Hunters grind for lookalike ends. Read more than first 4 and last 4 when it matters.
- A QR is data. Stickers get swapped. Scan, then read the confirm sheet.
- Dust in “recent” is not a friend. Do not send back to it.
- Checksum means internally consistent, not “this is Sam.”

Take the quiz. Then we send — gas, failed transactions, and the Approve button.

lessons.title: A send, step by step on BSC
lessons.content:
# A send, step by step on BSC

You will do this slowly, even when you are “sure.” A send is not a chat message. It is a signed instruction the book will keep.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to walk a native BNB send and a BEP-20 token send on BNB Smart Chain without mixing the dropdown, the asset, or the gas reserve.

## Native BNB send

1. Network = BNB Smart Chain. Chain id 56 if the app shows it. Not Ethereum. Not a testnet. Not “BNB Smart Chain (test).”
2. Paste address. Check first 6 and last 6 against the source you trust — the recipient’s receive screen, not a week-old chat.
3. Amount. Leave a little BNB for **this** fee and **future** fees if you still need to move tokens later.
4. Confirm. Wallet shows estimated gas in BNB. Read the destination on the sheet again.
5. Wait. Open BscScan. See success. Copy the **tx hash** — the long identifier of this instruction.
6. Only then tell the human on the other side “it is paid,” and give them the tx hash. Chat is not a receipt.

If the amount would annoy you to lose, insert a tiny test between steps 2 and 3. Test, explorer, remainder. You already know this ritual. Sending is where people skip it because they are “just paying a friend.” Friends still cannot reverse a wrong door.

## Token send (BEP-20)

Same as above, plus: you are calling the **token contract** to update balances. You still pay gas in **BNB**.

If gas is missing, the wallet will fail. If you are looking at Ethereum in the network dropdown, you may send a different asset or fail. Look at the dropdown every time. Crystal Stones, if you hold any, moves as a BEP-20 token on this book. This is not a buy order. It is a description of a send you might one day do with a practice amount.

USDT on BSC is also BEP-20. USDT on another chain is not this send. Say the full sentence before you tap.

TABLE
Field | What you verify | Failure if you skip
Network | BNB Smart Chain for this academy’s token path | Right letters, wrong book
Asset | BNB vs USDT vs Crystal Stones — pick on purpose | You paid in the thing you meant to keep
To | First/last 6 match the intended door | A hunter or a void
Amount | Test first if it hurts to be wrong | A beautiful mistake
Gas | BNB left over after the send | Tokens stranded
Tx hash | You can paste it into BscScan | A screenshot argument
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Sam sends “all” BNB including what would have paid the next token transfer.

1. The BNB send succeeds. BscScan is green.
2. Crystal Stones (or USDT BEP-20) still sits on the address and cannot move until more BNB arrives.
3. A stranger in a group chat offers to “unlock gas” if she pays a fee to their 0x. That is theft.
4. She obtains a little BNB from a venue she chose — an exchange she already uses, or a friend she can actually find — then moves the tokens.
5. She keeps a **gas reserve** after that. There is no honour in a zero-BNB wallet full of tokens. “Max” buttons are how people strand themselves.

DIAGRAM
Pick network (BSC, chain id 56)
  --> pick asset (BNB or a BEP-20 token)
    --> paste + check ends
      --> tiny test (if needed)
        --> explorer
          --> remainder
            --> keep BNB for next gas

Never: tell the recipient “paid” from a pending spinner.
Never: Max BNB if tokens still need a courier.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What you are actually signing

The wallet builds a transaction: to, value, data, gas parameters. You sign with the key. The RPC broadcasts. Validators include it in a block. BscScan reports the book. Your chat does not.

If you sign on the wrong network, you signed a different book’s instruction. If you sign to the wrong to, you signed a gift. If you sign an Approve thinking it is a send, you signed a loaded gun — two lessons from now.

Read the sheet. The sheet is the last honest place. A website can draw a smiley. The sheet shows the 0x.

NOTE
Never send your entire BNB balance if you still need to move tokens later. Leave a reserve. “Max” buttons are how people strand themselves. Nobody honest will ask you to Max-send BNB to “activate” Crystal Stones, and this academy will not ask you to send us a test as a graduation fee.
ENDNOTE


## Talking to the recipient like an adult

Do not say “I sent it” from a spinner. Say “here is the tx hash, check BscScan on BSC.” If they cannot use an explorer, walk them to the row, or wait until your own bookmark shows success to their door. If they insist on a screenshot of your wallet, that screenshot is still a report. Offer the hash.

If they gave you an address in a group chat and then a “corrected” address in a DM, stop. Confirm out of band. Poisoned corrections are a job. The send ritual includes knowing whose mouth the 0x came from.


## The Max button, again, because it will still be there

Max on a token send is less dangerous than Max on BNB, but it still deserves a look: are you emptying a token you needed to split, are you paying a hunter, are you on the right book? Max is not evil. Unread Max is. Leave BNB. Read the sheet. Then Max is just a number.

## What this lesson is for

You have a send ritual. Next: what gas actually pays for — gwei, why a failed transaction still costs, and why cheap-fee panic is how people get stuck.

## Say this out loud

- Dropdown first. Asset second. Ends third. Then amount. Then gas reserve. Then explorer. Then you may say “paid.”
- Token sends still spend BNB. A max BNB send can strand tokens.
- Tx hash is the receipt. Chat is not. A spinner is not.
- Practice amounts you can lose. A send is hard to reverse.
- The confirm sheet is the last honest place. Read the 0x.

Next: what gas actually pays for — gwei, failed tx still costs.

lessons.title: What gas actually pays for
lessons.content:
# What gas actually pays for

**Gas** is the fee the network charges to run your instruction. On BNB Smart Chain you pay it in **BNB**, the native coin. Tokens do not pay the courier. A pretty Crystal Stones balance does not move itself.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say why a failed transaction can still cost BNB, what **gwei** is doing on the sheet, and why “gas is high” is not a reason to type a seed into a discount site.

## The courier is a computer, not a bank clerk

A public chain has no branch manager who includes your payment out of kindness. People running software — **validators** on BSC’s current design — include transactions. Gas is how you pay for that inclusion and for the work of running the instruction.

**Gas limit** is the maximum work you allow the transaction to do. **Gas price** (often shown in **gwei**) is how much you pay per unit of that work. **Gwei** is a tiny unit of the native coin. You do not need to convert it in your head. You need to read the wallet’s estimate in BNB, and you need to keep extra BNB so the estimate is not your entire balance.

Simple BNB sends are cheap most days. Token transfers cost a bit more work. Approves cost work. Complicated contract calls cost more. You will not learn to hand-tune gas in Basic. You will learn not to panic-press settings you do not understand.

TABLE
You see | What it means | What to do
Estimated fee 0.0003 BNB | The app’s guess for this instruction | Keep more BNB than the guess
Failed, but BNB went down | The network ran the attempt; it still spent work | Read the error on BscScan; do not retry blindly into the same wall
Pending for a long time | May be underpriced, congested, or RPC lag | Wait; check explorer; do not double-send a second full amount
A site says “pay 0.5 BNB to unlock gas” | Theft | Get BNB from a venue you chose
Gas 0 because “we sponsor fees” | Maybe a genuine feature, often a lure | You still must not Approve a stranger
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Emeka tries to send USDT BEP-20 with almost no BNB.

1. The wallet estimates a fee he cannot cover. The send never starts — or it starts and fails.
2. He retries five times, each fail nibbling BNB he did not know he still had, or each pending stacking in the app.
3. A pop-up says his wallet is “frozen pending gas” and offers a wallet-connect unlock. That is a drainer.
4. The adult path: he stops clicking. He checks BscScan. He acquires a little BNB from an exchange he already uses. He sends once.
5. He leaves a reserve so the next token send is boring.

DIAGRAM
Your signed tx
      |
      v
RPC broadcasts
      |
      v
Validators include it if gas is enough
      |
      +--> success: state changes, you paid gas
      +--> fail: state may not change the token, you often still paid gas
      +--> pending: not in a block yet — wait, do not double-pay
ENDDIAGRAM

## Failed tx still costs — say it until it sticks

On EVM chains including BSC, a transaction that **runs out of gas** or **reverts** (the contract says no) can still charge you for the work done. The book did not credit your friend. The courier still worked. That feels unfair if you grew up with “failed transfer, no fee.” It is how this machine is built.

Read the explorer status: success, fail, pending. A red fail is not “nothing happened to my BNB.” Check the fee line. Then fix the actual cause — wrong token, missing BNB, contract error — before you retry.

Do not raise gas to “priority” because a stranger said you are stuck, then also send a second copy of the full amount. That is how people pay twice. The next lesson but one is about stuck transactions. Today: gas is BNB, failed can cost, strangers do not unlock it.

NOTE
Nobody honest needs your seed to “top up gas.” Nobody honest needs remote desktop to “set gwei.” If fees confuse you, wait, read BscScan, and move a practice amount. This academy will not sell you a gas-saver dApp.
ENDNOTE


## Why BNB must sit in the same address

Gas is paid by the **sending address**. A second wallet full of BNB does not pay for the first. Tokens on address A plus BNB on address B means A is still stuck. Move a little BNB to A, then move the tokens. Do not send the tokens to a stranger who “will add gas.”

This is also why a brand-new receive of only Crystal Stones, with 0 BNB, cannot leave. If someone airdrops you tokens and you have no BNB, you are not late to a listing. You are looking at bait you cannot even move without first fetching a courier from a venue you chose.


## Estimates lie a little, thieves lie a lot

An estimate of 0.0004 BNB that becomes 0.0005 is normal. An estimate of 0.0004 that a website rewrites into “send 0.4 BNB to this unlocker” is not an estimate. It is an invoice from a stranger. Gas is paid **inside** your transaction to the network, not as a separate pre-payment to a helper address.

If the wallet estimate is far above what BscScan shows for recent similar sends, you may be on the wrong network or a fake RPC. Stop. Bookmark. Recheck chain id 56.

## What this lesson is for

You know what the courier charges and that failure is not always free. Next: Approve — the permission that is not a send and still empties wallets.

## Say this out loud

- Gas on BNB Smart Chain is paid in BNB. Tokens do not pay the courier.
- Gwei is a small unit of price per work. Read the estimate in BNB. Keep a reserve.
- A failed transaction can still cost. Check the explorer fee line before you retry.
- “Pay gas to this address to unlock” is theft. Get BNB from a venue you chose.
- Do not double-send because a spinner is slow. Pending is not a dare.

Next: what Approve actually grants — the quiet way wallets get emptied.

lessons.title: What Approve actually grants
lessons.content:
# What Approve actually grants

On Ethereum-style chains (including BSC), many sites do not take your tokens immediately. They ask the wallet to **approve** a spender.

**Approve** means: you sign a permission for a **contract** to pull up to N tokens later, without asking you each time.

This is how swaps work. It is also how drainers work. By the end of this lesson you should read an Approve sheet as a loaded gun, not as a “continue” button.

## Permission, not payment, not a connection tick

Connecting a site usually shows your address to that site. Annoying, sometimes enough for targeted dust, not the same as spending. **Signing** a message can prove you hold a key. Sometimes harmless, sometimes a login, sometimes a trick. **Sending** moves coins now. **Approve** lets a program move tokens later.

If you do not know why a site needs an approval, **reject**. Prefer the amount you actually intend to swap, when the UI allows. Mystery “claim,” “airdrop,” “drainer reverse,” “support unlock” approvals are theft.

The spender is a contract address. It is not the friendly logo. If the sheet says unlimited, that is the next lesson. If the sheet says a token you did not mean to touch, reject. If the sheet appeared after you tapped a mystery Crystal Stones clone, reject.

TABLE
Prompt | Translation | Beginner move
Approve 50 USDT for a swap you started on a site you chose | Often legitimate if you chose the site | Read token, amount, spender; still not a command from this academy
Approve unlimited Crystal Stones for a site you just met | A loaded gun | Walk away
“Sign to verify wallet” that is actually Approve | A costume | Walk away
Permit / Increase Allowance | Same family as Approve — read it | Same rules
Set token allowance | Approve in other words | Same rules
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A Google ad says “Crystal Stones airdrop.” You connect.

1. It asks to Approve unlimited tokens. You sign because the logo looks right.
2. Nothing appears in your balance, or a fake balance appears.
3. Later the tokens leave. The chain shows you authorised a spender. Support cannot reverse an authorisation you signed.
4. The published Crystal Stones contract 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 was not a reason to Approve a stranger. Adding a token is viewing. Approving is permission to pull.
5. You rotate only if the seed itself leaked. If only an Approve leaked, the intermediate skill is **revoke** — later tracks. Until then: do not grant them to strangers. You cannot “un-sign” with a feeling.

DIAGRAM
Connect  (they see your address — usually not a spend)
   |
   v
Sign message  (proof of key — read it; still not always a spend)
   |
   v
Approve (they may take tokens later — danger)
   |
   v
Swap / transfer (the actual move, plus gas in BNB)
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why this exists at all

Decentralized exchanges cannot take tokens from you without a permission, unless you send to them. The Approve design lets a contract pull the input of a swap. That is a real use. Drainers copy the same popup. The popup is not a halo. The site you typed from a bookmark is the context. A sponsored ad is not a bookmark.

This academy will not walk you through a swap as homework. Swaps are how people skip the rest of Basic and meet drainers early. If you already know you need a swap, you still read the sheet: which token, how much, which spender, is it unlimited.

NOTE
Revoking approvals is an intermediate skill (a later track). Until then: do not grant them to strangers. You cannot “un-sign” with a feeling. Academy staff will never ask you to Approve a “verification spender,” and will never send a dApp link in a DM.
ENDNOTE


## How to read the sheet without becoming an engineer

The wallet sheet usually shows a token icon, a number, and a spender. The number may look like a send amount. It is often an **allowance** — a ceiling, not a purchase. If you hold 20 USDT and approve 20, the spender may pull 20 later, maybe not now. If you hold 20 and approve unlimited, the spender may pull 20 now and whatever arrives tomorrow.

If the token on the sheet is not the token you meant, reject. Drainers ask for a valuable token while the website talks about a worthless airdrop. If the spender address is not a venue you can name, reject. You do not need to decode the contract. You need to refuse unknown spenders.

A hardware device will still show Approve. Read that screen too. The box does not translate “unlimited” into “safe.” It translates your confirmation into a signature.

## Practice amounts still need this lesson

People think a 2 USDT wallet cannot teach Approve. It can. Drainers take what is there and wait if they have unlimited. A practice wallet that you later reuse as a funded wallet carries old allowances. That is why this academy prefers: do not Approve strangers even with dust, and treat a practice wallet you Approved on as dirtier than it looks.

If you already Approved a mystery site, stop using that wallet for new deposits until you learn revoke on a later track — or rotate if you also leaked a seed. Name which object was compromised: allowance versus combination. They are different playbooks.

## What this lesson is for

You can name Approve as permission to pull later. Next: why unlimited approvals exist, and why convenience is not an argument for a site you met today.

## Say this out loud

- Approve means permission for a contract to pull tokens later. It is not a simple send and not a connection tick.
- Unlimited plus unknown site means no. Claim sites that need approvals are usually drainers.
- Adding Crystal Stones by contract is viewing. Approving a clone is how real tokens leave.
- Connect is not approve. Approve is not send. Read the wallet sheet.
- You cannot reverse an authorisation with a support ticket. The book shows you signed.

Next: unlimited approvals and why they exist.

lessons.title: Unlimited approvals and why they exist
lessons.content:
# Unlimited approvals and why they exist

An **unlimited approval** is an allowance so large it might as well be “all you ever hold of this token, including what you receive tomorrow.”

Sites ask for it so you do not have to sign a new Approve every time you swap. That is convenience. If that contract is malicious, or later hacked, or later sold, it can pull until you are empty without a new popup.

By the end of this lesson you should treat unlimited as a deliberate trust decision, not as a default tick, and you should know that “everyone signs unlimited” is not a safety argument.

## Convenience versus blast radius

A capped approve — 50 USDT for a 50 USDT swap — means the spender can take at most that much unless you approve again. Slightly more clicks. Much smaller blast radius if the site is wrong.

An unlimited approve means you are saying: I trust this program with this token for the life of this permission, including future deposits. That can be reasonable for a venue you have researched like an adult. It is not reasonable for an airdrop, a Google ad, a “Crystal Stones staking” page you met in WhatsApp, or a site that opened itself.

Phishing pages copy the same “unlimited” checkbox because it pays. One signature, many later withdrawals. Bots watch allowances. Speed is their product.

TABLE
Situation | Unlimited? | Why
A swap you started, UI lets you set 50 USDT | Prefer 50 | Matches the job
A DEX you already use, you understand the trade | Maybe, as a later choice | Still a trust decision, not a law
A site you met today with a logo you like | No | Logos are cheap
“Approve to revoke a hack” | No | Drainers love this costume
“Approve to receive airdrop” | No | Receiving does not need your allowance
Hardware wallet in the mix | Still no to strangers | Hardware does not fix a bad Approve
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Riley uses a swap site she chose. The sheet asks for unlimited USDT.

1. She looks for an amount field. Some UIs hide it behind “custom.” She sets the swap amount, not unlimited.
2. If the UI refuses to work without unlimited, she decides whether this venue is worth that trust. “It refused” is information, not a command.
3. A second tab pops up from an ad, also asking unlimited Crystal Stones. She closes it. She did not start that job.
4. Weeks later the first site is fine and the ad site would have emptied her. BscScan would have shown her signature on the allowance, not a mysterious hacker.
5. She still keeps a gas reserve in BNB, because none of this is free to unwind later.

DIAGRAM
Capped approve
   50 USDT allowance --> spender can pull <= 50
   later deposit of 200 USDT --> spender still capped at remaining allowance

Unlimited approve
   2^256 style number --> spender can pull until you are empty
   later deposit --> still pullable without a new sheet
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why wallets default to easy

Apps compete on fewer clicks. Fewer clicks include dangerous defaults. You are the adult in the loop. This academy will nag you about the sheet more than about yield, because yield is not our subject and the sheet is how beginners get wrecked.

Revoke tools exist. They are a later skill, they cost gas, and fake revoke sites are drainers wearing a mop. Until you can name a revoke tool from a source you already trust, the control you have is **not granting**.

NOTE
“Everyone signs unlimited” is how whole group chats get emptied in one afternoon. This academy will not tell you that unlimited is always evil. It will tell you it is a loaded gun, and that a site you did not choose does not get to hold it.
ENDNOTE


## The huge number is not a compliment

You will see a figure with dozens of zeros. That is not “the site is rich.” That is the ceiling they want. Some UIs write “Max” or “Infinite.” Same gun. Some write a token’s whole supply. Same gun. Read past the logo.

If you are practising, you do not need a DEX this week. You can finish Basic without a swap. The people who “just try a swap” on a sponsored site are how unlimited gets its reputation. Curiosity is not a venue.

When a later course shows a swap, you will still bring this sentence: **how much, of which token, to which spender, for how long.** Unlimited is “how long = until I revoke or I am empty.” Capped is “how long = until this amount is used.”

A token you added as a view — Crystal Stones on the published contract — can still be the asset an unlimited Approve targets. Viewing did not invite that. Do not Approve Crystal Stones to a site you met in a blast, even if the blast used our name.


## Tomorrow’s deposit is in the blast radius

Unlimited is not only about what you hold tonight. If you get paid next month into the same address, the old spender may still be allowed to pull. That is the convenience: you do not re-Approve. That is the danger: you forget who you trusted in March. Capped amounts forget for you.

If you use one hot wallet for experiments, keep the pile you would miss on a different seed. Experiments collect allowances. Allowances collect endings.

## What this lesson is for

You now know why the huge number exists and why you should not feed it to strangers. Next: failed, pending, and stuck transactions — the spinner that makes people double-pay.

## Say this out loud

- Unlimited means this spender can pull this token until you revoke or you are empty, including future deposits.
- Convenience is why it exists. Drainers are why it is famous.
- Prefer a capped amount when the UI allows. If it does not allow, that is a trust decision, not an order.
- Hardware does not make unlimited safe. You still signed the gun.
- Fake revoke sites are drainers. Not granting is the Basic control.

Next: failed, pending, and stuck transactions.

lessons.title: Failed, pending, and stuck transactions
lessons.content:
# Failed, pending, and stuck transactions

A spinner is not a verdict. BscScan is.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to tell **pending**, **failed**, and **success** apart, and you should know the two beginner sins: paying twice, and handing a stranger remote desktop “to unstick it.”

## Three statuses, three jobs

**Pending** means the network has not put the instruction in a block yet — or your RPC has not seen that block. Wait. Check the explorer with the tx hash. Do not assume it is lost after forty seconds. Do not assume it succeeded because the app played a happy sound.

**Failed** (reverted, out of gas, status 0 on the explorer) means the instruction was included but did not do the thing you wanted. You may still have paid gas. Fix the cause. Do not immediately resend the full amount to a slightly different address a helper invented.

**Success** means the book changed as that instruction specified. Confirm it is the instruction you meant: asset, to, amount. Then you may tell the human.

**Stuck** is a pending that sits. Causes include: gas too low for the moment, RPC lag, a nonce gap (a previous pending from the same address is blocking later ones), or you are watching the wrong network. You do not need to master **nonce** — it is a sequence number so your address’s transactions stay in order — but you need to know that a second send while one is pending can queue or collide in ways that scare you.

TABLE
Status on BscScan | What you do | What you do not do
Pending | Wait, refresh explorer, keep the tx hash | Send the full amount again because WhatsApp is impatient
Success | Tell the recipient, with hash | Also send a “just in case” copy
Failed | Read the error, fix cause, then one retry | Approve a “stuck transaction fixer” dApp
Not found | Wrong explorer, wrong network, or never broadcast | Paste the seed into a broadcast helper
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Amaka sends USDT BEP-20. The app says pending. The recipient says they have not been paid.

1. She copies the tx hash. She opens BscScan from a bookmark, on BSC, not a DM link.
2. If pending, she waits. She does not send a second 100 USDT. She may message the hash so the recipient can watch the same row.
3. If the explorer cannot find the hash, she checks the network and the RPC. She still does not type her seed into a “push transaction” site.
4. If it failed, she checks whether she has BNB, whether the token is the right contract, whether the to address is right. Then one corrected send.
5. A helper offers AnyDesk to “speed up gas.” She refuses. Remote desktop plus a wallet is how the helper sends for her.

DIAGRAM
Broadcast
   |
   v
Pending ----> included ----> success (state changed as instructed)
   |              |
   |              +----> failed (included, job not done, gas often gone)
   |
   +----> still pending (wait; do not double-pay)
   |
   +----> never seen (wrong book / RPC / you cancelled)

Stranger with remote desktop sits outside this diagram, holding your pen.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Speed-up and cancel are advanced

Some wallets offer **speed up** (same job, higher fee) or **cancel** (a dummy transaction with the same nonce). Those are useful and easy to botch. In Basic, prefer waiting on a practice amount. If you must act, stay inside the official wallet’s own speed-up, and still watch the explorer. Do not import the seed into a second “stuck tx” app.

A replacement transaction is not a time machine for a success. If the first one landed, speeding up does not unsay it.

NOTE
Remote desktop, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, “share screen so I can set gwei” — academy staff will never ask. A pending transaction is a wait, not an invitation. Practice amounts exist so that waiting is tolerable.
ENDNOTE


## Nonce, without a maths class

**Nonce** is a counter: your address’s next transaction number. If tx 7 is pending, tx 8 may wait. If you then fire tx 8 with a full second payment, you may have two live jobs. If 7 lands and 8 also lands, you paid twice. If you replace 7 with a speed-up, you need the wallet to keep the numbers straight. That is why Basic says wait.

You do not set nonce by hand in this course. You do notice: several pendings from one address is a reason to stop tapping, not a reason to import the seed into a “nonce fixer.”

## The recipient’s clock is not the network’s clock

WhatsApp impatience is not a status. A recipient who says “I have not received” may be on the wrong network, watching a watch-only of the wrong address, or looking at a delayed RPC. Send them the tx hash. If BscScan shows success to their door on the right book, you are paid. If it shows pending, you are both waiting. If it shows a different to, you have a different problem — and a second send will not unsay the first.

Practice amounts make waiting cheap. That is why they exist.


## Two explorers, same hash

If a stranger’s explorer link and your bookmark disagree, your bookmark wins. If your wallet and your bookmark disagree, wait and refresh the bookmark. If two honest statuses remain pending, you wait. The only thing that turns pending into two successes is your second send. That is the one move this lesson exists to stop.

## What this lesson is for

You can sit with a spinner without donating a second copy. Next: connect versus sign versus send, so the last sheet you see in a dApp is a named object.

## Say this out loud

- Pending, failed, and success are explorer words. A spinner is not.
- Failed can still cost gas. Success is not “whatever I intended.” It is what the instruction said.
- Do not double-send a pending payment. Share the tx hash instead.
- Remote desktop to unstick a wallet is how the wallet leaves.
- Speed-up and cancel are advanced; wait on practice amounts.

Next: connect versus sign versus send — three different permissions on one screen.

lessons.title: Connect versus sign versus send
lessons.content:
# Connect versus sign versus send

Three different popups wear similar colours. Beginners mash them into “I clicked yes.” Drainers depend on that mash.

By the end of this lesson you should name which permission you are giving before your finger moves, and you should reject anything you cannot name.

## Connect

**Connect** (WalletConnect or an injected-wallet connect) usually means: this site can see my address and may ask me for more signatures later. It is not a send. It is not an Approve. It is still a tracking door. Connect to sites you chose. Disconnect when you are done if the wallet makes that easy. Connecting to a random “Crystal Stones portal” gives the portal a target.

WalletConnect is a protocol for linking a phone wallet to a website. The honest version shows a pairing you started. The dishonest version is a QR from a DM. If you did not start the pairing, do not scan it.

## Sign

**Sign** a message means: prove I hold the key that controls this address, or agree to some text. Some logins use it. Some scams use it to trick you into a **permit** — a gasless-style allowance. If the sign sheet looks like a novel, or mentions spending, or mentions unlimited, treat it as Approve’s cousin. If you cannot explain the message, reject.

Signing is not “free so it must be safe.” Free of BNB is not free of consequence.

## Send (and Approve, which is a kind of send)

**Send** is a transaction that costs gas and, if successful, changes the book: BNB moved, tokens moved, or an allowance set. **Approve** is a send to a token contract that writes permission. Both show a fee in BNB. Both deserve the full read: network, asset, to, amount.

If a site says “sign to continue” and the wallet sheet shows a network fee, you are in send-land, not in a free login. Believe the sheet, not the website caption.

TABLE
Sheet | Typical cost | What they get | Beginner test
Connect | Usually none | Your address, a chance to ask for more | Did I open this site on purpose?
Sign message | Usually none | Proof of key, sometimes a permit | Can I explain this sentence?
Send BNB / token | BNB gas | Coins moved now | First 6 last 6, asset, network
Approve / permit | BNB gas or a signature | Right to pull later | Do I want this spender to take this token?
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A “support agent” sends a WalletConnect QR so they can “raise your BNB Smart Chain limit.”

1. Amaka did not start a pairing. She does not scan it.
2. If she had scanned, the next sheet might be Connect (already too much), then Sign, then Approve unlimited.
3. She names each sheet out loud. If she cannot, she rejects.
4. Real academy support, real wallet brands, real exchanges do not raise limits by QR from a chat. They do not need her seed, her 2FA, or her desktop.
5. She reports the account and goes back to her bookmark.

DIAGRAM
You opened a site from a bookmark
        |
        v
Connect?  only if you want that site to know your 0x
        |
        v
Sign?     only if you can explain the message
        |
        v
Send / Approve?  only if network, asset, to, amount are the job you started

DM QR / pop-up / sponsored ad
        |
        v
Reject. You did not start a job.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Say the name out loud before you tap

This is the whole skill. “This is Connect.” “This is a message signature.” “This is Approve unlimited USDT.” “This is a BNB send to 0xabc…def.” If the sentence will not come, the tap should not happen.

Practice on a site you do not need, with an empty wallet, if you like — still not a dare to import a funded seed. Module 6’s lab stays on official apps and practice amounts. DApp tourism is not the lab.

NOTE
Crystal Stones Academy will never ask you to Connect, Sign, or Approve to collect a certificate, to unlock a lesson, or to “sync progress.” Progress lives on our course account, not on your keys. A wallet sheet in our name is a costume.
ENDNOTE


## Disconnect is a habit, not a cleansing ritual

Disconnecting a site does not revoke an Approve you already signed. It only stops that browser session from nagging you as easily. If you Approved, you still have an allowance until you revoke or the tokens leave. Name the object: session versus allowance versus seed.

After this lab, disconnect sites you do not use. It is hygiene. It is not a time machine. The checklist in Module 5 includes this on purpose.


## A worked rejection script

When a sheet appears, say: “This is Connect to a site I opened / did not open.” If you did not open it, reject. If you did, continue. Next sheet: “This is a message. I can / cannot explain it.” If you cannot, reject. Next sheet: “This is Send of X on BSC to 0x…ends, or this is Approve of token Y unlimited to a spender I cannot name.” If that sentence includes unlimited and an unnamed spender, reject.

Practise the script on an empty wallet if you wish. Do not practise it by importing rent. The script is the skill. The tap is optional.

## What this lesson is for

You can name the three permissions. Take the quiz. Then hardware, household, and inheritance — the signer as a tool, the backup as a family object.

## Say this out loud

- Connect shows your address. Sign proves a key or may hide a permit. Send and Approve change the book or the allowance.
- Believe the wallet sheet, not the website caption. A fee means you are in send-land.
- WalletConnect QRs from DMs are not support. If you did not start the pairing, do not scan.
- Name the permission out loud. If you cannot name it, reject it.
- Academy certificates do not need a wallet signature.

Take the quiz. Then hardware, household, and inheritance — without worship and without folklore.
